The Paramokṣanirāsakārikā composed by Sadyojyotiḥ Śivācārya,
together with the commentary composed by Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha.
That goal which those learned in Sāṃkhya and Yoga have attained through delusion,
those learned in the knowledge of Vedānta desire as the Vedic goal.
Those who are devoted to the Pāñcarātra, those who are great lords among yogins, and those who are the authors of the Pramāṇa-āgneya, the Viśikha, and the Amalakāraka;
"Those others who propound liberation while remaining established in impurity speak falsely.
Thus ends the Raurava-sūtra.
Having thus established the preeminence of the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta), [the text now proceeds] to the proof of the fruit of initiation (dīkṣā).

Now, in order to demonstrate by way of contrast the results proclaimed in other systems— both similar and dissimilar— the meaning of the two and a half sūtras beginning with "those who know Sāṃkhya and Yoga" is stated in verse:
"For him whose collection of limbs has been described as being for the sake of purifying the existent (sattva)..."
The description of the fruit which has been stated is for the purpose of distinguishing it from that fruit [of worldly action]. || 1 ||

For one to whom the hands of Śiva and other limbs have previously been bestowed, that initiation—distinguished as "existent" because it is the cause of liberation through the exclusion of non-yoga (ayogavyavaccheda) by virtue of its being a non-conjunction with what is improper—has a fruit which will be described:

the manifestation of one's own qualities such as omniscience upon the cessation of all bonds. It is through the differentiation of that [initiation] that [the fruits] sung in other tantras [are explained].

The fruits [of the means] are now described. He will state the purpose for explaining these distinctions among the fruits in the conclusion, beginning with the verse "In their means" (Śloka 59). || 1 ||
Therein, he indicates them in sequence:
"Isolation, enjoyment of the *sattva*, dissolution into the Supreme Self, and subsistence within the unmanifest and so forth—these are indeed dissolutions among the evolutes. (2)

Indeed, the soul's connection with *prakṛti*, characterized by the three *guṇas*, is the cause of its non-isolation (*akevalatā*). And this is not merely a spatial connection, because since both [the soul and *prakṛti*] are all-pervasive, that [mere connection] would exist even in the state of isolation (*kaivalya*), which would result in the impossibility of such a state. Rather, it is an eternal relationship consisting of the enjoyer and the enjoyed, whose nature is the failure to realize their distinction.
Because the state of being an enjoyer consists in the non-discrimination of the intellect (*pratyaya*), as they say: "Experience (*bhoga*) is the non-discrimination of the intellect.

For primordial nature (*prakṛti*), even while offering herself as an object of enjoyment to the Spirit (*puruṣa*), offers her in such a way through the conjunction with the powers of ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), and so forth—which are essentially afflictions acquired through the capacity of *tamas*.

Just as one does not develop the notion that the remnants of a meal consisting of food from a clever courtesan are to be abandoned, so too [the yogi] would not develop the notion that the remaining transformations are to be abandoned; otherwise, since no bondage other than those [transformations] could be established, experience would be impossible, and there would follow the consequence of the absence of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). And it is precisely that latent impression which is said to be the adversary of liberation (*kaivalya*).

But when, through self-knowledge or through yoga, discernment (*viveka*) shines forth for that person in its own luminous nature, untinged by anything else, then— because non-discernment has been utterly destroyed as its very opposite— the expansion consisting of that [non-discernment] does not arise toward it; and upon the cessation of Prakṛti’s state as an object of enjoyment in every respect, his supreme isolation (*kaivalya*) is attained.
"Emancipation"—thus say the most eminent experts in that scripture.

He states another result with the words beginning "the enjoyment of *sattva*": the connection with *prakṛti* is indeed beginningless. That the Puruṣa is the enjoyer is accepted by all; nor is that state of being an enjoyer merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), for if it were so, he would not possess it [as his essential nature].

It might be argued that [bondage and liberation] could belong to another, but since it is impossible for a dharma performed by one to result in the transgression of the obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) of another, or if such a transference were to occur, that person would not be the experiencer; thus, to whom would bondage or liberation belong?

Therefore, the state of being an experiencer (*bhoktṛtva*) must be accepted as constituting one's very nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, the destruction of that which is beginningless and eternal in its nature is not logical, because if it were so, it would follow that even the *puruṣa* itself would possess such a quality, resulting in the fallacy of nihilism (*vaināśikatva*).
Precisely because its destruction is impossible, the relationship between the enjoyer and the enjoyed must be admitted to exist even in liberation for the Puruṣa and Prakṛti.

It was only due to the wickedness of beginningless karma that Prakṛti previously became his object of enjoyment, taking the form of a dissolution into pleasure that was obscured by pain and delusion. As for the cessation of all karmas which serve as the cause of that [bondage], from which [cessation] liberation arises—

"This [Self]—whose nature is pure, uninterrupted, unsurpassed, unlimited existence, consciousness, and bliss—is the object of enjoyment; therefore, those who have attained it are called 'enjoyers of existence' (*sattvabhuj*). This is the introductory framework (*pīṭhabandha*) for those who know the tradition of that [scripture]. "Dissolution into the Supreme Self" is the fruit according to other scriptures, such as: "All this is indeed Brahman" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 3.14).
1) From the Vedic testimony characterized by the statement, "There is no diversity whatsoever here" (*Kaṭhopaniṣad* 4.11; *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad* 4.4.19),

which attains its authority by having as its object an already established reality (*siddhārtha*)— an authoritative scripture (*āgama*) that, being non-human in origin, is more powerful than other scriptures— and from this [scripture], one understands the nature of His qualities, such as supreme bliss and so forth, which are sung in various parts of that same scripture, [one realizes] that He is not accessible through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*).

Because the Brahman-consciousness, which is undivided by objects of perception, is real, while all other things consisting of duality have as their sole essence a construction of ignorance (avidyā) and are therefore unreal, there is this realization. For this very reason, they say: "Since the Self is self-evident, the seers declare it to be so. And there is no [need for] further investigation of this realization.

When difference (*bheda*) is sublated by perception and other means of valid cognition that establish [the absence of] existence, its lack of authority must be suspected—just as in the case of the statement "one should sprinkle with fire"—because difference, being dependent on mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) and conventional recognition, cannot be established as an object of perception which grasps only the thing-in-itself (*vastumātra*);
for it is unreal, being imagined solely through ignorance (*avidyā*), like the horn of a hare. As it has been said: "Perception is said to be an affirmer" (*bra0 si0*).

2 |1) Thus it is said. And this being so, although the individual souls (jīvātman) possess as their essence the true Supreme Self— which is established by its own authority and has been proclaimed— nevertheless, because they are deluded due to being defiled by ignorance (avidyā), their mental states consisting of dream-experiences are like those of a person who is fast asleep.
Due to the non-arising of authentic awakening, the manifold world of differentiation called "saṃsāra"— which fails to bring about the cognition of that [true] nature—

is, by its very essence, not for the first time [in this life]. However, at some point, through the attainment of a more intensely powerful knowledge according to the sequence taught in scriptures such as "The Self is to be known," and by uprooting the causes of delusion which are the opposites of that [knowledge], all delusion is cast aside.

The realization of the Supreme Self—like that of one who has awakened from sleep—is established in its own essential nature alone; it consists in the dissolution of the previous stream of the individual self (*jīvātman*). This very state is considered by some to be the supreme liberation (*parā mukti*).
Now, one might object: here, the intention of the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*) is clearly the mature Vedānta doctrine, and not the doctrine of Māyā.

"That very [theory] is the establishment of [its] status as the material cause" (Śloka 49)—this follows the refutation that is about to be stated. It is true that it follows that [refutation]; however, this is not proclaimed as the primary view in the Vedāntas by the foremost among those who know the inner self (adhyātmavid). Nor are there scriptural passages (śruti) here that accord with it. And how that very [theory] follows the refutation, we shall explain right here.

The phrase "in the unmanifested, etc. is an indication of the results according to other scriptures. That wherein the most subtle individual knowers (kṣetrajñas) abide together with their karmas is called the unmanifested (avyākṛta). Where do they abide? Regarding this, some say: just as here [in the world], in things associated with clay...

Since you observe that jars and other such objects are effects of clay, you maintain that even in the case of causes and effects associated with pleasure and so forth, pleasure and the like must be accepted as the primary cause in their respective forms. In exactly the same way, although there is a difference between individual selves and the primal matter (*pradhāna*), let it be accepted that they have a single cause, because the persistence of a single essence (*sattā*) is possible; or else, let this [single causality] not be accepted here.

Because there is no distinction among them, that which is their cause is the supreme *prakṛti*, designated as the Great Sovereignty (*mahāvibhūti*); it is insentient because it is the cause of the insentient. That very [cause] transforms itself directly into the fourfold nature characterized by the Lord, into the nature of the non-lordly individual soul (*kṣetrajña*), and into the form of insentient ignorance (*avidyā*). Knowledge (*vidyā*), however, consists of the intellect (*buddhi*) and mind (*manas*); due to the absence of distinction, it exists as the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).

And because the elements are [derived] from the specific differentiation of the primary element (bhūta), the elements exist as the sense organs; thus, in this sequence, that very [Prakṛti] transforms in such and such ways, and therefore she possesses supremacy. As they say: "The Blessed Vāsudeva is the supreme Prakṛti, the preeminent manifestation, and indeed the manifestation itself. He himself becomes the past and the future," and so on, by virtue of his subtlety, his non-pervasiveness, and his pervasiveness within that very [Prakṛti].

Because they are effects, the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) persist; for it is from that very material cause, which is subject to transformation, that the individual selves (jīvātman) arise through the continuous connection with ignorance and karma. Upon the exhaustion of that [ignorance], their dissolution into that supreme causal self—the nature of which is the complete subsiding of all differentiated effects—is the highest good.

For some, this is a difficult position to accept. By the inclusion of the term "among the indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) and so forth, those who maintain the doctrine of dissolution into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*) are included; likewise, those situated below them who maintain the dissolution of the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*) and the rest are the Tāuṣṭikas. As it has been said: "The internal [contentments] are four, known as Nature (*prakṛti*), Means (*upādāna*), Time (*kāla*), and Fortune (*bhāgya*); the external are five, resulting from withdrawal from sense-objects—thus nine contentments have been declared."
Thus [ends the verse from] Sāṃkhyakārikā 50. || 2 ||
The great host of Maheśa is indeed not the agent, though it knows all that is to be known;
even in the state of agency, it possesses a state of being directed [by Him], for it is equal to the treasury of splendors.

The other fruit is the attainment of *sālokya*, *sāmīpya*, and so forth. As it is stated in the *Pauṣkara*: "By other initiations here, liberation (*nirvāṇa*) is not attained; by them, the state of *Gāṇapatya* [is reached]. And this very point is indicated by the Sūtra-author through the term 'yogin'. The fruit of the other philosophical systems is that "the knower of all objects of knowledge is a non-agent. In the case of the Supreme Lord, however, there is the status of being both the object and the agent of action.

It has been established through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for effects such as the body, the senses, and the world. This being the case, the impossibility of otherwise accounting for effects no longer serves to establish the agency of a liberated person (*muktapuruṣa*). If it is argued that agency is established for the liberated one because they are liberated like God (*īśvara*), that is incorrect; for God’s state of liberation is unproven and thus cannot serve as an example. Indeed, it is the bound who is liberated.
There is an absolute dissimilarity between the Lord (*īśvara*) and the perfected ones (*siddha*) in certain respects. As the venerable Avadhūta stated in the *Vyāsākṣiṇī*:

"The distinction is that although Paramaśiva has ceased his office with respect to the perfected ones, he has not ceased his office with respect to others; whereas the perfected one has, in every respect, entirely ceased his office. Nor do they say that the person possesses agency even prior [to liberation].

However, as in the Sāṃkhya position, that [agency] belongs to *prakṛti* alone; thus, since there is no evidence for agency in liberation, there is indeed non-agency. Knowledge (*jñāna*), however, is established as innate to the person (*pums*) from prior experience. That [knowledge], being free from obscuration in liberation, becomes all-encompassing; therefore, those who know the scriptures maintain that the liberated one is a non-agent who possesses knowledge of all objects. In this context, the author of the Sūtras has introduced [the Puruṣa] by the term "author of the means of knowledge" (*pramāṇakartṛtva*), because he is the author of such works as the *Hṛdayapramāṇa*.

Furthermore, according to another tradition, even in the case of being an agent, there is the state of being directed (*prayojyatva*). This is the meaning: just like the quality of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*), agency (*kartṛtva*) is also the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the Person (*puruṣa*).
It is not logical for Prakṛti to possess agency, because she is the cause (*kāraṇatva*); for causality is indeed something else.

In insentient objects, the nature of change in essential form—such as transformation—is invariably present by their very nature, as is established by direct perception in cases such as milk turning into curd. Furthermore, agency consists in independence, characterized by the desire for the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful; it is the cause of the engagement and withdrawal of all other causal factors, and is invariably concomitant with the state of Śiva-hood.

We shall state in the *Mantravārttika* that this is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Furthermore, the agency of selves has already been proven by means of inference in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and other works by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*). Now, one might object: "If agency exists in selves, would they not then be subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitā*) by virtue of having the nature of motion (*spanda*)? No; for agency is not established as having the nature of motion. For motion is indeed action (*kriyā*).
Nor is the agent's agency defined by the nature of an action, for that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress through the postulation of further agents.
Rather, it exists there solely as a cause, since the movement of the body and its instruments is observed precisely through its power.
How could a movement consisting of an action that pervades insentient matter belong to an agent who is invariably characterized by the pervasion of consciousness? And it is not...

The state of being an agent (*kārakatva*) consists not merely in the nature of vibration (*spandātmakatā*), but rather in the possession of a specific power (*viśi�ṣṭaśaktiyoga*), as in the case of magnets and the like; this has been stated by us elsewhere: "That power which exists in the vibration-action of inert matter is established as the agency of consciousness, which is all-pervasive and established in the form of vibration by itself, like a magnet. And that agency is established for them as being from beginningless time through its being impelled by the Lord (*īśvara*).

Since destruction is impossible for that which is beginningless, those who know its principles maintain that the liberated ones—being auspicious, omniscient, and omnipotent—are indeed directed by Paramaśiva.

The result of other philosophical systems is the attainment of equality with the sun and fire, as seen in the statement "equality through proximity to light"; such equality with the sun, fire, and so forth is taught in their respective scriptures.
For this is heard in the Mahopaniṣad and other texts, and these have been designated by the author of the Sūtras as having Agni as their agent. || 3 ||
Supremacy over the Supreme Lord and absolute purity belong exclusively to the Siddha; indeed, agency and indifference belong to the Great Lord (Maheśvara).

Another consequence [of this view] is that, because the Supreme Lord is admitted to possess the authority over dissolution (*laya*), the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*) cannot be removed due to the persistence of the bondage of authority and so forth. As they say: "Favor (*anugraha*) and concealment (*tirobhāva*) are the two bonds belonging to Sadāśiva," and "The first bound soul is Sadāśiva. This is because all bonds have been withdrawn, and the authority over states such as dissolution has been set aside.

In every respect, for the self that has been established as free from limiting adjuncts (*anupādhi*), there is an even more excellent state of deficiency [of suffering]. Others, however, claim that the liberation described in the *Pātañjala* [Yoga] system is merely hinted at [here]. For them, since that [liberation] was already included by the term *kaivalya* (isolation), just like the liberation of the Sāṃkhya, the charge of redundancy is unavoidable. Indeed, there is no difference between the two types of liberation, because in both cases it consists of the disjunction from primordial matter (*prakṛti*).

For this very reason they say: "Sāṃkhya and Yoga are one" (Bhagavad Gītā 5.5). However, there is a difference in the means: for in one [system] knowledge is the means thereto, while in the other it is practice; enough with this elaboration. And it is precisely this superiority that was expressed by the author of the Sūtras through the term *maheśvara*. Furthermore, regarding purity (*nirmalatva*), the word *kevala* indicates that liberation is merely the cessation of impurity (*malanivṛtti*), and not—

The manifestation of omniscience and other qualities is also impossible, because there is no evidence for their existence prior to such manifestation; for it is the case that only what already exists can be manifested—this is the intended meaning. Indeed, the Great Lord’s agency and indifference are already established. As the author of the Sūtras said: "He is devoid of instruments and material causes. For the Supreme Lord engages in the creation of the world solely for the sake of others.

Having perceived that the perfected being (*siddha*) who has attained the state of universal agency is equal to himself, [the Lord] realizes at that very moment that his own agency would become differentiated; consequently, due to the fault of the resulting lack of restriction in all actions because of the possibility of multiple agents, he understands that this would instead be a cause for failing to accomplish the welfare of others. Having withdrawn that [agency], he remains indifferent as his own self. Thus is the *Siddha*.

Furthermore, the proponents of the doctrine of a perpetually flowing Lord (pravāhanityeśvara) argue as follows: having understood that the Lord has spoken out of a lack of intent to accomplish the welfare of others, and perceiving that the fulfillment of all goals for others cannot occur without an omniscient creator, they maintain that [the Lord] assumes the state of being the creator of all things solely out of compassion.
Endowed with the performance of good deeds, he dwells in the world of the stars;
there occurs the destruction of both knowledge and agency, as well as another [state] which is the destruction of everything.
The person (*puruṣa*), being beginningless, transmigrates in a continuous stream, bound by effects and instruments;

since destruction of that which is beginningless is impossible, there is no means of valid cognition for the non-existence of effects and instruments in liberation, except for the cessation of the body, senses, and suffering caused by karma as observed in the state of worldly existence.

The wicked intention of some is that liberation for the selves consists in their abiding in the path of the stars (nakṣatramārga) within the world of the stars (*tārakā-bhuvana*), due to the attainment of performing even more excellent actions; they claim it is the destruction of both knowledge and agency. They argue that since there is an absence of intellect (*buddhi*) in liberation, there is an absence of desire and effort, and thus the destruction of agency as well as the non-existence of the intellect and so forth.
Because of the absence of the nine qualities of the self.

As they say: "Apavarga is the absolute liberation from the nine—namely, intellect (*buddhi*), pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), desire (*icchā*), aversion (*dveṣa*), effort (*prayatna*), mental impression (*saṃskāra*), merit (*dharma*), and demerit (*adharma*)"; likewise, another [definition] is the destruction of everything.

Because consciousness has the singular nature of being the grasper (*grāhaka*), and because this state of being a grasper exists only in dependence upon an object to be grasped (*grāhya*), and because that object—

due to the impossibility of its existence in any way through conceptual alternatives such as atomic or gross— is non-substantial, the state of being a grasper which depends upon it is likewise illusory; thus, for those who maintain the doctrine of the "extinguishing of a lamp," its destruction occurs simply through the arising of a subverting cognition (*bādhajñāna*).

Thus [it is said]. Others, however, out of dullness accept this position: that consciousness arises from the elements themselves and perishes along with them; thus, with the destruction of the body, there is the total destruction [of the self]. || 5 ||
Having thus demonstrated the results well-known in other tantras, he concludes: "In this way, liberation has been conceptualized by disputants according to their own systems;
however, the actual equality with the true Lord has never been seen by those blinded by delusion. (6)

By those blinded by various forms of delusion, whose mental eyes are overcome by ignorance, that fruit characterized as liberation—which is accessible solely through the scriptures concerning the Lord (pati) and is defined by equality with the truly existent Supreme Lord—has not been seen. Therefore, they have imagined such a liberation through their own conceptual constructions. || 6 ||

Now he speaks to those who follow the Samatā-tantra: "And equality, through the positions of arising, transition, and penetration, is proclaimed as the supreme manifestation, which is beyond the reach of intellect and speech. (7)

The *Gītā* is supreme (*parā*) because it is an expression of equality with the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), whose nature is the manifestation of qualities such as omniscience. Why is it supreme? He says: "Because of the positions of arising, transference, and possession" (*samutpatti-saṃkrānti-āveśa-pakṣataḥ*). This is because, in the state of being a bound soul (*paśu*), qualities such as omniscience do not exist; and in the state of liberation (*mukti*), the scriptural testimony regarding equality with the Supreme Lord would otherwise be inexplicable.

Some accept the position of equality through origination, asserting that at that time, a previously non-existent set of qualities such as omniscience arises in the self of the liberated soul, equal to those of the Supreme Lord. Likewise, others adopt the position of total transference, maintaining that the qualities of the Supreme Lord are transferred to the liberated soul, just as the fragrance of musk transfers to a cloth. By this [it is shown]:

The Pāśupatas, who maintain the doctrine of the transference of the crest (*śikhā-saṃkrānti-vādinaḥ*), have been described by the author of the Sūtras as being "those who make [the body] crestless" (*viśikhākāraka*). According to others, however, there is the position of "possession" (*āveśapakṣa*), wherein the perfected one is entered by the very qualities of the Supreme Lord residing in their own substratum, just as a person is possessed by spirits (*graha*).
Distinct from these alternative positions regarding equality with the Lord, this equality of manifestation (*abhivyakti-samatā*) will be discussed hereafter.
It is "supreme" because it is beyond the range of both intellect and speech.
Having thus pointed out the fruits of other tantras, he refutes them according to the sequence of their meaning: "The enjoyer of beings and the dweller among the stars—these two are perishable;
and the enjoyer who dwells in the worlds is seen in the world to be perishable. (8)

The two results—being an enjoyer of beings and dwelling in the stars—are both perishable; for the destruction of an enjoyer who dwells in the worlds, such as Devadatta and others, is observed. Now, one might object: "But being an enjoyer is simply being a knower, which is the very nature of the *puruṣa*; how then can it be said here that this non-fruit of action perishes? If that were so, then the *puruṣa* would be omniscient, and not merely a knower of the *sattva*.

Since there is no specific reason [to the contrary], let it be our very own view. [Objection: "Granted that this may be so, how can the connection of the inhabitants of the worlds with the worlds and so forth—which are beginningless by way of a continuous stream—be terminated? Therefore, because of this beginninglessness of the stream, the eternal nature of things situated in their respective states cannot be overturned by actions or their various fruits; such is the ultimate truth. (8)

The leaders of the Gaṇas, though equal to fire, must be impelled because their desires are not yet fully realized; for one who does not act is indeed unsuccessful, since there is no one equal to the Lord.

In this regard, there is a refutation of these two positions: "the great host of Maheśa" and "equality with the treasury of splendors" (verse 3). First, concerning [the claim of] equality with the Lord of the Gaṇas: since there exists a higher state, the desire for that attainment remains present; thus, because his wish is not yet fulfilled, how can there be liberation? The same applies to the cases of equality with Agni and Āditya.

This should be examined. Now, if you claim that the omniscient and omnipotent creator is someone else entirely, who is not perceived by people such as ourselves—just like fire, the sun, and so forth—then if that were the case, liberation would consist in attaining equality with Him; thus, there is no fault, as this is precisely our own view. By the phrase "and non-agent," these two positions are set aside: [1] that the non-agent is one who knows all that is to be known, and [2] that even if there is agency, it is a state of being impelled (by another). "In that same way" means just as...
The two lords of the Gaṇas (Nandin and Bhṛṅgin) are said to have their desires fully realized;

likewise, these two [the two Śivas] are also not liberated despite being omniscient, because their desires are unfulfilled due to their longing for the state of having the Supreme Lord as their co-creator. For liberation is indeed the attainment of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Agency, like knowledge, belongs to the person (*puruṣa*).
It has been stated that [the soul's state] is its very own nature; therefore, in the absence of attaining that [nature], how can there be liberation? Let it be so [that there is no liberation];

however, how and when could the state of being impelled by the Mantreśvaras—which belongs to souls from time immemorial—ever cease, since it is the cause of bondage, just like *kalā* and the other [categories]?
And because that [impulsion] does not cease, this [soul] too, being subject to being impelled like the Vidyeśvaras, remains indeed unliberated. || 9 ||
He presents the position that [the soul] has superiority over the Supreme Lord (in verse 4) as follows:

"If there were superiority, there would be an absence of means and an impossibility due to the two paths; furthermore, the state of being subject to effort in the Supreme Lord would result without any cause. (Verse 10)

The non-existence of a means of proof (*sādhanāsattva*) constitutes the absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*). For no superior state of the selves is established by any means of valid cognition through the attainment of the manifestation of their own stainless and most excellent qualities in the form of omniscience and omnipotence, such that upon reaching it, a superiority of Īśvara could be described in liberation. But was it not said regarding Īśvara?
It is argued that a deficiency is established through the immersion (*samāveśa*) into states such as dissolution (*laya*). Now, what is this "immersion into a state"?

If it is a separate entity, that is not accepted, because the deity is one. How so? Because [the idea of] a transformation of attributes (*dharmapariṇati*) has been previously refuted on account of the defect of non-consciousness (*acaitanya*), and it will be refuted again. If it is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), that too is not possible, because it would be unreal. Whence could it have the nature of that [deity]?
The power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which exists inseparably from the agent and is situated within the agent itself, illuminates the state of Śiva;

it assumes there the status of a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) denoted by terms such as "absorption" (*laya*). When that very power is engaged in the accomplishment of an effect and has not yet reached the transformation resulting from the completion of that effect, it then illuminates the state of Sadāśiva.

It becomes the cause for being denoted by words such as "enjoyment" (bhoga) and so forth. Indeed, when the collection of effects has been accomplished and the offices that awaken [the soul] have ceased, it then assumes the status of a cause for the application of terms such as "Lord" (Īśvara).

Thus, in this context, the conventional usage of difference is based solely on the diversity of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of those respective effects; there is no real difference in the entity itself.
The Gurus, who are experts in discerning the true scriptures, maintain that the positions of *vivarta* (illusory manifestation) and *pariṇāma* (transformation) are absolutely impossible. As they say:
"For the expression 'the form' and 'the possessor of the form' is merely a figurative statement regarding power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*)" (*Tattvasaṃgraha*, verse 50).
Therefore, even though this scripture consists of five streams, there is no difference in the deity, because it is a single unity; rather, [there is only a difference in the aspects].

[The Lord] is to be worshipped as possessing only those forms [of the fivefold activities], distinguished by the fivefold functions such as creation, maintenance, and so forth. Otherwise, there would be the consequence of a division of scriptures here—just as in the case of the Kaula Mahāvrata and other systems—which would contradict the scriptural declarations of His oneness. Furthermore, if one were to accept that the established [Lord] undergoes states such as dissolution as previously described, He would not be seen as the agent; on the contrary, His inferiority to Īśvara would be asserted.
There would be no excess [of power].
Now, as for that which is the supreme lordship of even Īśvara—the power consisting of omniscience and the like, which is the nature of light without limiting adjuncts (nirupādhi), as they say:
"Salutations to her by whom even he is not omniscient without her"—that is more excellent than the state of Parameśvara.

It is argued that [the goal] is accepted as something to be attained by means of a *siddha* (accomplished being); however, this is incorrect, because the distinction between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*) is unestablished, since the designation of their difference is merely conceptual. Since lordship (*īśvaratva*) is of the same nature as the power of omniscience and so forth, a mutual difference between them is not logical; thus, they possess an undivided essence. Nevertheless, the verbal distinction is not sublated, and it is through that [distinction] that the determination of the object proceeds. This is also true for power.

The excellence of that capacity, and the further excellence of that excellence—liberation being such a state of even greater excellence—would result in a lack of finality for liberation itself, because there would be no fixed limit to the gradations of excellence to be established by terms such as "more" (*taratama*) and so forth.
A mere distinction based on conceptual designation does not lead to any cessation [of progression]. Therefore, it must be equal to the Lord (*īśvara*).

Liberation is to be accepted [as the state], but not an increase [in qualities]. The agency consisting of the power to bestow grace and to cause concealment is not of the nature of a bond (*pāśa*), because it is a specific form of agency and is free from limiting adjuncts (*anau-pādhika*). Furthermore, as for that "state of being a bound soul" (*paśutva*) mentioned by you, it is intended to establish the manifestation of another power through the conceptualization of a distinction based on ego-inflation (*ābhimānika-bheda-kalpanā*), for the sake of one established upon the seat of yoga (*yogapīṭha*).

This should be explained through the lens of figurative interpretation by means of a comprehensive examination of all the scriptures, possessing the state of the sacred seat (pīṭha) of the Blessed Lord Sadāśiva as set forth in the *Mantra-bhāṣya*; one must not, however, insist upon a literal understanding of the words alone. Enough, then, with disputing with those who have not served a guru and who are full of scriptural meanings fabricated by their own imagination.
Alternatively, the statement "the animal (paśu) is primordial Sadāśiva" is said without any figurative usage, with the intention of referring to the Sadāśiva who is to be consecrated.

For it is thus: in initiation, for one who has been extracted from the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), there occurs a gradual manifestation of the state of Śiva—which consists of the power of action (kriyāśakti)—preceded by the destruction of impurities, according to the distinctions of gross, subtle, and supreme.
The manifestation of the essential nature of the various states of the Lord of Mantras (*vidyeśvara*), while being brought about,

is in reality the cause for attaining the three principles (*tattva*) that are distinct from one another— namely, the forms of Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śiva. Since, in that state of Sadāśiva, the state of being impelled has not ceased, and because *mala* still exists as a mere specific residual impression (*saṃskāra-mātra-viśeṣa*), the condition of being a bound soul (*paśutva*) has not yet been removed.

"Because the word 'animal' (paśu) is applied [to these] without figurative usage. And this the author of the Commentary (*vṛttikāra*) will state with the words beginning, "For at the end of initiation, where could they possibly exist? etc. However, regarding the *sādāśiva* [level], which is purificatory, its being so [called as an 'animal'] is stated to be figurative, because in the ultimate sense there is no possibility of a difference from Śiva. He states that there is yet another defect in this position: "And the non-abiding [of the soul occurs] due to the two paths."

Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, there is the consequence of an infinite regress here through two paths. Regarding that, he states by one path: "the state of being impelled" (*paryatvam*). Now, if the state of being impelled were established for the Supreme Lord even without a cause, then the status of being the Supreme Lord would result [only] for the Siddha; for at that time, due to that very superiority, the Siddha himself would be the Supreme Lord. Otherwise, the mention of that superiority for the Siddha would be entirely fruitless.

It might be argued that even for that Siddheśvara, if he were to attain another Siddhānta, he would become non-supreme; and for him too there would be yet another, leading to an infinite regress regarding the Supreme Lord—this is the meaning. || 10 ||
With the second argument, he says:
"And this conceptualization of a cause by living beings is futile;
for does a person become a Lord merely by being free from impurity? (11)

This conceptualization of the self as "I am God" by those seeking liberation—wherein one imagines oneself to be God as a causal agent for the sake of attaining the state of being God—is a volition that would be fruitless, devoid of purpose, and unstable. The implication is that no one would strive for the sake of liberation from saṃsāra. Now, [the text discusses] its stainlessness:

He refutes the position [stated in] verse 4 with the words "merely by purity" (*vaimalyamātreṇa*). Since the bound soul (*paśu*) possesses limited knowledge and the Lord (*pati*) possesses omniscience, one must admit that [the state in question] is distinct from both; yet, because it is pure and its power of cognition has not been experienced as such through its purity, is this liberation—which would be of the nature of a non-human goal—not something like a stone, amounting to nothing at all? This is the underlying intention: [The intended meaning is: ... [as above].
Since the self possesses the very nature of being a knower as will be explained later, if that [nature] were not admitted, there would be the fault of its destruction; as he will say:
"Those for whom their own self perishes are the foremost among fools" (verse 57). || 11 ||

He refutes the position that "agency is indeed established" (Śloka 4), etc., with the following: "Why would the Lord not be an agent out of fear of a multitude of causes? Since the simultaneous liberation of many [souls] is inevitable, that [agency] remains indeed unavoidable. (12)

For the status of being an agent (kārakatva) arose from the Blessed One who was already established; why, then, for what reason, is this not accepted in the case of another person being established? The proponent of the prima facie view states the reason: "out of fear of a multitude of causes.
A multitude (anīka) of causes is their collection, that is, their plurality; fear arises from that. For instance, as for one who is [already] established...

At that time, since the status of being the creator of all has already been fulfilled by [the individual souls], if the Supreme Lord were also to possess the status of a creator, then his creativity would be distinct [from theirs]. Consequently, with the possibility of multiple creators, there would be a confusion in the creation of the universe, such as [the thought]: "Let this be new," or "Let this be old.
Fearing this, [the opponent] maintains [his position]. To this, the proponent of this system replies: "Of many," because the causal capacity is inconceivable.

When many persons are liberated simultaneously, then, because each one possesses the capacity for universal agency once their purpose has been fulfilled, there would be no distinction in their agency due to their equality. Since it is impossible to establish a fixed status for any one of them, if agency were established through a collective combination (*samuccaya*), that very [agency] which bestows the diversity of the creation of the universe and so forth would remain [unchanged]. There is fear regarding the multiplicity of causes. Now, this proponent—

Because the error of human cognition arises from causes such as greed and passion, once that is determined, he will—through the absence of passion and so forth in liberation, and by means of the application of manifold powers—avoid the calamity of creating the world through erroneous cognition;
the underlying intention is that he will thus come to reflect upon our very own doctrine. || 12 ||
Now he refutes the results [claimed by] the Samānatāntrikas:
"Furthermore, there is impermanence in the case of origination; through possession (āveśa), there is a lack of independence;
and there is no existence of an example for proving the transference of qualities. (13)

In the view of those who maintain that liberation consists in the arising of equality with the universal [Lord]—namely, the equality of qualities such as omniscience and so forth—in their system, liberation is impermanent because it is something produced and thus subject to origination. Regarding the theory of "possession" (*āveśa*): liberation occurs through the infusion of the Lord’s qualities; even in this position of equality, the liberated person lacks independence, just like one possessed by a spirit, and thus their "equality with the Lord" is merely nominal. As for the position of equality through "transference" (*saṃkrānti*)...

He refutes [the opponent's position], stating that there is no valid example [to support it]: "The qualities of the Lord transfer into liberation"—this transfer of qualities is not established by perception for you, because those [qualities] are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).
If it is argued that this is known through inference (*anumāna*), that is incorrect; for in the inference that establishes the transfer of qualities, there is no example.
Because the existence of an example is necessary, and inference does not proceed without an example due to the impossibility of establishing a universal concomitance (*vyāpti*),
the proponent of transference (*saṃkrāntivādin*) here states an example: "Indeed, in the transference of one's own cognition, the instruction of words is observed."
In the scripture, the transference of consciousness is prescribed; it shall bring success to the practitioner. || 14 ||
The object of the disciple is perceived by the gurus through instruction for the purpose of transferring their own realization.
In this scripture as well, beginning with the *Svāyambhuva*, the transfer of knowledge (*jñānasaṃkrānti*) is heard of in the context of the initiation of an ācārya:
"This authority which has been transferred by me to you today must be exercised by you until it has been transferred to another."
(Svāyambhuva 24.21). But how is that [transformation] possible if the transference of qualities is not admitted?
In this regard, the illustrative example is established by both your own scripture and direct perception. || 14 ||
The proponent of the established doctrine says:
"But from instruction, another such consciousness arises;
it does not fail because of the similarity of the word 'transference' [applied] to that of the teacher. (15)

Due to instruction and its cause, another cognition—entirely similar [to the previous one]—arises in the disciple's intellect as if it had been transferred, but there is no actual transfer of that very [same] cognition. Why? He says: "Because of that" (tad). That knowledge does not depart from the teacher. For if the position of transfer were true, then because the knowledge would have been transferred to the disciple, it would be absent in the teacher.
It may be so. || 15 ||
In the scripture as well, the meaning of the term *saṃkrānti* is precisely "independence" regarding exposition and so forth, due to the command of the Guru and because he explains like a Guru.

Likewise, it has been established by the Guru himself in the *Svāyambhuva* and other texts within the section on the initiation of the Ācārya; thus, he says that *saṃkrānti* is not established here [in the ordinary sense].
By the command of the Guru, one's autonomy regarding the scripture should be as it was with the Guru;
the meaning of the statement concerning "transference" was explained by the Guru in that very context. (16)

Now, if at some point an advocate of transference (*saṃkrāntivādī*) should object, due to the confusion between the illustration and the illustrated subject established by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, [the author] says the following to refute that as well by means of the extension of the logic of the illustration:
"In the same way, from the reviling of a virtuous person, demerit or merit is produced."
And their own merit is exhausted when they act perversely toward one who possesses patience.

And so says the Smṛti: "From reviling virtuous twice-born men, or from associating with sinners, sin is transferred to men and their own merit departs. Likewise: "In one who is patient, through the absence of abuse and by dwelling with the meritorious, merit is transferred to men and sin departs elsewhere."
Thus, the aforementioned examples have been refuted as before. || 17 ||

Since even here, the very arising of new merit and demerit is what is called "transference" (saṃkrānti), and not the actual movement of those two themselves— for otherwise, the injunctions for acquiring merit would result in futility by merely coexisting with the removal of the fruit,
and the instruction on expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) would be rendered meaningless— he says:
From association with the wicked, another evil is born;
likewise, from those who possess merit, merit arises—it has been declared that it is not otherwise.
The proponent of transference (saṃkrāntivādī) removes the suspicion regarding the illustrative example by stating:
"The production of another lamp from a lamp [occurs] in relation to another fuel, such as the wick and so forth, which are to be consumed."
The transmigration of that [self] is not at all accepted by the Buddhists, the Vaiśeṣikas, and others. (19)

In this case as well, since it is observed that a very great fire, such as a forest conflagration, arises from nothing more than the flame of a lamp, the production of something previously non-existent (*apūrvotpatti*) alone is established by all schools of thought, including the Buddhists; however, the transference (*saṃkrānti*) of that [fire] in its entirety or even of a portion of it is not logically tenable. By this, the delusion regarding the transference of the fragrance of musk and the like onto cloth and other materials should be refuted.
The proponent of transmigration (saṃkrāntivādī) states another example: "Is it not the case that the transmigration of 'cowness' and so forth extends to other individuals?
This [argument] does not hold for one for whom cowness and so forth consist of similarity. (20)

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) refutes similarity by arguing that since the universal is perceived at the very moment a particular cow is born, and since it was not perceived prior to that moment, it must have been non-existent there; and if one does not admit its migration from another individual, its connection with this new one would be impossible—therefore, migration must necessarily be accepted. Thus, he rejects the notion of similarity.

Regarding the phrase "of which": for us, the transference of a universal (*sāmānya*) is not established, because we do not accept a universal distinct from the individual (*vyakti*), as the Sāṃkhyas do; rather, similarity consisting of a single part is what constitutes the universal. Consequently, there is no possibility of suspecting a transference [of a universal] into a cow-individual born at that very moment, since in this case the similarity of another individual has arisen from the individual itself.
Because suchness would be untenable. || 20 ||
It has been stated that transmigration occurs precisely through the non-existence of another universal; however, this being said in response to that [position] does not appear appropriate.
Therefore, with the intention of addressing the proponent of a universal distinct from the individual (vyakti), he says:
"For that [universal], though pervading its own substratum, is manifested within the substratum despite the difference [of individuals]."
For one for whom spreading is not accepted, how could there be transference? || 21 ||

Since the possibility of a transfer [of the universal] does not arise under the view that the universal is omnipresent (*sarvagata*), he says here—relying on the view that the universal resides in the individual (*vyaktigatasāmānya*)—"even though there is difference" (*bhede 'pi*). This means that even when the substratum (*āśraya*) has arisen as something distinct at that moment, [the universal] is manifested.

Because the universal is manifested by those individuals, and because the individuals possess a single nature (*ekasvabhāva*) consisting of manifesting it, [the universal is apprehended] through them and not from anything else.
Regarding transmigration (*saṃkrānti*), he states another reason: "pervasion" (*visarpaṇa*). || 21 ||
Furthermore, regarding the transmigration of that which is formless, neither the world nor the investigator accepts it;
for since they admit that a universal is both inactive and formless, how could it possess the capacity for transmigration?
Indeed, this is established neither by worldly consensus nor by the consensus of the learned.

Now, having provisionally accepted the transfer of the lamp and its universal, he says: "The quality of being a universal does not exist in the universal, nor does it exist in the lamp; therefore, that which was stated is futile. (22)
The meaning is this: the proponent of transference (saṃkrāntivādin) must strive to establish that [transference] by means of an illustration of the transference of qualities.
However, even if the transference of a universal (sāmānya) and of a lamp were established, since those two do not possess the nature of a quality, they cannot serve as illustrations in this case;
therefore, their description is utterly fruitless. || 22 ||
He rejects another example:
"The transfer of water from one field to another is possible because it is a substance;
for that power resides only in a substance, like a whetstone or a sword. (23)

In the case of the water of the sacred site (tīrtha) called Kedāra, a transition (*saṃkrānti*) [of its power] is indeed admitted when there is another person who uses it simultaneously with the person who consumed it, because it is a substance (*dravyatvāt*). He provides an illustration: "like a perfected sword" (*siddhakṛpāṇavat*). For a perfected sword, even though it remains at a very great distance from the perfected one, passes into his very hand through the connection with him, since the powers of substances are inconceivable.
This is the meaning.

For this very reason, because the proof of transference (*saṃkrānti*) is established through inference based on a power proven by an extremely marvelous illustration, the water of a field (*kedāravāri*)—that is, the water from a cultivated plot—is not to be explained here as the subject of transference; for when a matter is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no need for inference.
It proceeds. || 23 ||

Thus, having established that the proponent of transmigration (*saṃkrāntivādin*) lacks a valid example, the proponent of transmigration now objects by taking a thing established in his own system as the example:
"For it is indeed intended that the quality (*guṇa*) resides in both conscious and unconscious entities."
Otherwise, the engagement with the function of a real entity would not be logically possible. || 24 ||
Although both *cit* (consciousness) and *cetana-śakti* (the power of consciousness) are qualities (*guṇa*), you maintain that they reside in non-conscious entities (*acid-vastu*).

Why? He says: "Not otherwise" (*nānyathā*). Otherwise, if that [power] were not its object, the activity of that non-conscious entity toward the result to be accomplished would not be possible. This is what is meant: the presence of both knowledge and action must be admitted to reside in the agent as well as in the object; for [activity] is not connected with mere consciousness (*cid-ananvita*).

Because there would be an incapacity for activity due to being inactive (*syācita*), and because all things abide solely within their own self-nature, it would be impossible for them to serve as a substratum for mutual conjunction; thus, even if they were objects of knowledge, no specific quality such as "being an effect" could exist [in them]. Yet, we observe that insentient causal substances, such as clay and the like, when influenced by the power of a potter or similar agents, [do indeed produce effects].
Since it has been stated that this is a "particularity" (viśeṣa), the presence of the power of consciousness (cicchakti) therein must necessarily be admitted. || 24 ||
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:

"Let it be desired that even when [the state] is established, there is the emergence of the qualities of the Supreme Lord; because they were previously non-existent, but now, due to the manifestation of great majesty... (25)
By this very reasoning, even though [the soul] is established [as being essentially free], let the persistence of the quality belonging to the Supreme Lord be accepted.
However, such a quality is not seen to belong to the perfected one (siddha) by its own nature even previously; thus he says: "Because of non-existence previously" (*prāgasattvāt*).
Previously, in the state of a bound soul (*paśu*), the limited collection of qualities such as knowledge and agency did not exist for him; but now, however—

In the state of perfection (*siddhāvasthā*), it is heard that [the power] is limited by the convention (*samaya*) of its Lord. Nor is it logical to say that what was merely limited has become unlimited, because of the contradiction [involved] and because it would entail the consequence of being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitā*). Furthermore, the emergence of something that was non-existent at that time is not tenable, since it has been stated to be indestructible. Therefore, by process of elimination, it is only a quality of the Lord that exists there in such a manner at that time.
The Pāśupatas [maintain] that it is transmigration. || 25 ||
Anticipating this objection from the opponent, he refutes it:

"For a quality that exists in isolation does not indeed subsist in another object; however, for that same quality when it has mounted upon its own substratum, such subsistence may occur figuratively. (26)

It is not tenable to assert that this quality of consciousness (*cit*), which consists of knowledge and action, can abide in another entity that is devoid of consciousness (*cic-chūnya*)—an entity that has become an object of perception—once it has abandoned its own possessor (*svaguṇin*). For if that were the case, that [devoid entity] too would possess the status of a knower and an agent;
consequently, all things would be sentient and all would be lords (*īśvara*), since everything is perceived by the Lord. However, [this is not so].

Even though that [agent], which resides in its own qualities, does not actually undergo modification when it exists in another substratum that is subject to modification, its persistence there is observed through metaphorical designation, not in a primary sense. Causality is simply the state of being capable;

and since this capacity of the agent with respect to the object is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), the postulation of the existence of that capacity therein is made.

It is indeed fruitless. Nor is it logical for the action of the agent to reside in the object, because that would contradict the reasoning already stated. Rather, by the force of that [action], the state of being so [as an action] is metaphorically attributed to it as well, due to the arising of vibration therein. || 36 ||
He provides an illustration: "Just as the quality of heat, though residing in fire, manifests intensely in water, so too does the quality of Īśāna manifest within that very [water]. (27)

Heat is the specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of fire; it is not appropriate for water, because that would lead to the undesirable consequence of a confusion among the elements. For earth and the other elements are distinguished from one another by their respective causes, such as support, cohesion, and digestion. Thus, heat is not a quality of water acquired through conjunction with fire, but rather resides in the fire itself. In that case, [heat] exists in water in an unmanifest form (*anudbhūtarūpa*).

Just as fire, being perceived, performs its own effects such as burning by means of the persistence of its own quality, touch, [the author] states the illustrative case with the word "tathā" (so too). Similarly, even a quality belonging to the Supreme Lord, while remaining situated in its own substratum, will be capable of producing various modifications in another substratum; thus, there is no reason for postulating its actual presence therein. 27
Thus, whether it be the position of possession or indeed the state of presiding,
for one who has not attained the transfer of the qualities (guṇas), he is as good as unborn or dead.

Regarding the two positions—the position of supreme immersion (*paramāveśapakṣa*) or the position of the presiding subject (*adhiṣṭhātṛpakṣa*)—which were introduced in the verse stating "even in the state of agency, there is the status of being impelled" (Śloka 3), he says "for the position... to show that these two are not like the position of transference (*saṃkrāntipakṣa*): "He is dead as soon as he is born."
Why is this? He says: "For even there, Śambhu alone knows everything and performs everything;
he is not established by his own qualities, because of the perception of his transcendence. (29)

It is not only in the case of possession (*āveśa*), but even in the case of transference (*saṃkrānti*), the Lord who has attained perfection through his own qualities knows everything and ordains everything, whereas the perfected being (*siddha*) does not; for it is never observed that one person, by means of another's action belonging to someone else, becomes either a knower or an agent. || 29 ||
And if, through contact with Him, even a perfected being (siddha) becomes all-creating and all-knowing, then it follows that even those who are insentient would attain the vision of all objects. (30)
The objection raised is: "From contact with that. If it is argued that even a perfected being (*siddha*) becomes such [omniscient] through contact with the qualities of Śambhu? The opponent replies:

This would apply even to insentient things. Since there is no difference in the nature of their contact with Him—because even insentient things like *māyā* and so forth are objects of the Lord's knowledge—it would follow that they too possess omniscience. || 30 ||

The prior non-existence [of the capacity] is unproven; moreover, the power of cognition and action is observed to be clearly enhanced through excellence, as it is manifested from its latent state. (31)

This is the refutation of the argument presented by others regarding prior non-existence. As for what was stated—that the capacity of the self for omniscience and so forth did not exist in its pre-existent state—that non-existence is unproven; because even in that prior state, their power of cognition and action was observed through the performance of effects that manifest them, such as [the production of] their own [cognitions], just as it is in the case of the self where...
The meaning is as follows: since the self is perceived in various bodies that manifest it, its pervasiveness is understood; likewise, the existence and pervasiveness of its qualities are established.
Just as it was previously established, so too is the manifestation of objects by the manifestor, such as light.

It is observed that for one who produces perfected ointments and the like, which stimulate the power of the cognitive organs; for one who effects skill in the organs of action through arts, crafts, and the like; and for one who masters the mind through the practice of yoga—their own inherent strength, consisting of knowledge and agency, is progressively enhanced according to each respective case. || 31 ||
To the question "Why?", he says:
"For in liberation, the Śāmbhava power is seen to be the manifestor of all objects;
therefore, by what can its equality [with that power] be prevented? (32)

Since the manifested [nature] is established as being of such a state through its connection with a more excellent manifestor characterized by liberation and lordship, who can prevent its equality with the Lord, given that its qualities are manifested in the same manner as those of the Lord? Furthermore, its manifestation and non-manifestation are caused respectively by the absence and presence of obscuration (*āvaraṇa*), and not otherwise.
Because it is refuted by that which effects a change in essential nature, thereby resulting in the state of being subject to transformation. || 32 ||
Having thus cleared away the objections against his own position, he states another fault in that of the opponent:

"The transition to another substratum without the abandonment of the previous substratum is simply not established; yet, if there were abandonment, the former [substratum] would be devoid of its qualities. (33)

For the transference of the sun and other luminaries is observed to occur only through the abandonment of a previous substratum and the entry into another substratum; likewise here too, if the abandonment of the previous substratum were admitted, that former [state] would become the supreme Śiva, devoid of all qualities, since the transference of those qualities would have already been established.
[The opponent objects: "But surely, it will have its occurrence in its own substratum, or there may be a transfer of it to another substratum, just like the light of a lamp. To this he says:
"For that song, as it moves, indeed spreads by leaving that [original place] behind."
And consequently, because it is not dedicated [to enlightenment], a host of faults will descend upon it. (34)

For it is held that when the production of a lamp has occurred, the light of that lamp spreads through various places by dispelling its own opposite, darkness; this is logical because it possesses the nature of transformation (*pariṇāma*), just like the flow of water. Furthermore, whatever form of the Supreme Lord’s attribute is subject to transformation is seen to be non-conscious (*acetana*), like clay and so forth; thus, there follows a multitude of faults to be mentioned later, such as lack of consciousness.
The consequence. || 34 ||

In whatever manner the establishment of transition is maintained as residing in a substance, that [establishment], which is proven by all means of valid cognition, is contradicted by the functioning of qualities. (35)

Alternatively, even if the proponent of transference (*saṃkrāntivādin*) has refuted logic, he is liberated from the epilepsy (*apasmāra*) of being overcome by transference because of the cutting off of the obsession with transference and so forth; yet, even so, that transference—which is brought about by the power of qualities such as virtue and sovereignty—is contradictory. Here, the transference of substances (*dravyasaṃkrānti*) is appropriate, for the transference of substances is well-established, but [the transference of qualities] is not.
Since [the qualities] originate from that [substance], it follows that the qualities of God would consequently entail the status of being substances themselves. This is the sense. || 35 ||
If it is argued that this fault does not apply if [the self] is a genus (*jāti*), then it is not so; for that [self] is indeed a quality such as cognition and the like.
If it were a substance (*dravya*), there would be the burden of postulating [an entity] distinct from the substratum of cognition and the rest. (36)

"Let it be then that qualities such as omniscience and the like, being established as residing in multiple individuals who are perfected lords, constitute a universal of quality (*guṇajāti*). This being the case, when that [universal] has attained the state of perfection in one person, its transfer to another person will occur—just as the whiteness of a jasmine flower [is perceived elsewhere]—and thus there is no fault whatsoever in the establishment of such a transfer. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it: "No."
For that [nature] consists of qualities such as knowledge; since the transference of these is not established, this argument amounts to nothing.

This is because even the qualities of jasmine and the like arise at that very moment. Furthermore, if this proponent should desire the transference of a portion of the substance *Īśvara*, which is the substratum of qualities such as omniscience, he says—refuting that it is likewise untenable—"In the case of being a substance," and so forth.

Thus, if substantiality (*dravyatva*) were admitted, the conceptualization [of God] as the substratum of cognition and so forth would entail an excessive burden (*gaurava*), which would have to be accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). To explain: the Lord would consist of a manifold collection of multiple substances; and upon the attainment of each respective established state of that substance, there would be a transition from that [state], and of that...
The postulation that [the Self] is the substratum of knowledge and so forth would be without proof and would result in an infinite number of imagined entities. || 36 ||

The proponent of transference (saṃkrāntivādī) states a fault in the liberation of the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin): "In that case, if liberation occurs through manifestation, it would be dependent on human effort (pauruṣa) and not Śāmbhava;
conversely, if liberation occurs through transference, it would be Śāmbhava and not dependent on human effort. (37)

Now, if it is the case that these very qualities (*guṇas*) are manifested for the person (*puruṣa*) in liberation, then—just as in the injunction "the Self is to be known"—liberation would follow as being the work of the *puruṣa* alone according to you as well, and not the work of God (*īśvara*), because His agency in that regard is untenable if He does not come into contact with those [qualities]. For if there were contact, there would necessarily be a transfer [of qualities]. To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) replies:
"In that case, it would indeed be Śāmbhava. || 37 ||

Even in your view, no one is liberated, because liberation would consist merely in the transfer of a quality of the Supreme Lord that already existed previously, and thus would not be connected to the person [who is supposedly liberated]. However, in my view, both [liberation and bondage] are tenable; as he says:
"The *pauruṣa* [liberation] has the person as its substratum, while the *śāmbhava* is created by Śambhu."
Which two are worshipped in manifestation, and which two indeed at the transition? || 38 ||

Liberation is designated as distinct because it is connected to two factors characterized by agency and object—the [agency] inherent in the person and the [action] whose agent is the Supreme Lord—just as one says "the cooking of rice" or "the cooking of Devadatta. Nor is it correct to argue that agency is not possible without a transfer [of action]. || 38 ||

The proponent of the final view (siddhāntavādin) himself states that his own position is what must be proven: "Let it be accepted that manifestation alone [is the object], for that is well-known along with its manifestors;
in it, nothing new or unseen is postulated. (39)

For it has been stated that the manifestation of the qualities of the Self is well-established along with their manifestors; let that very [manifestation] be accepted even in the case of liberation. My conception follows the analogy [of this]. Furthermore, the necessity of searching for analogies and so forth does not apply here as it does in your position. || 39 ||
The proponent of transmigration says:
"Since an impure quality of the person was observed previously, why is that same person, being thus [impure], desired as something preeminent? (40)

For manifestation occurs through the recognition of that very form, as in the case of a jar or similar object by means of a lamp or other light. However, in this context, prior to the state of perfection (*siddhi*), the quality (*guṇa*) of persons is established as impure and having limited objects; whereas in liberation, it is heard in scripture to be of a different nature—absolutely pure and equal to the Supreme Lord. Thus, because of the difference between these two states, [the former is] prior.
"Because recognition is impossible, we do not accept manifestation [of the self] in liberation. The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) says: "The person (puruṣa) as well...
Even from your perspective, the person is impure, since he has now become a vessel for the transmission of the attributes of the Supreme Lord.

Here is the opponent's intention: "If that [Self] is perfected through purification, why are its qualities not likewise desired? How can that atom, possessing such qualities, be pure in every respect even now? (41)

Now, if it is maintained by you that even though this [Self] is impure at that time, it becomes pure through the purifying operation of Īśvara—such as initiation (dīkṣā) and so forth—then how can its qualities be thus pure, since they are not pure with respect to all objects? To this he says: "The qualities...
Nor has it been said that those qualities do not exist previously; for although they exist, they are like darkness characterized by the veil of ignorance.

If manifestation occurs through cessation [of impurity], then for the sake of the cessation of all impurities, purity and impurity—being properties belonging to another (the *puruṣa*)—do not constitute a contradiction to non-difference;

thus, the rejection of liberation as manifestation is not tenable. Furthermore, he states that under the theory of transference (*saṃkrānti*), there is never any purity for the *puruṣa*, by saying "the atom" (*aṇu*). Just as the atomic self was previously endowed with qualities during its state as a bound soul (*paśu*).

Such impure qualities of its own nature persist even now; since you admit that there is a further excellence of those qualities in liberation, how could it be pure in every respect? The meaning is: it certainly is not. || 41 ||

Regarding the point that even if the purification of its personal qualities is not admitted, we certainly accept the purification of the substance alone—which serves as the locus for the transference of the Lord’s qualities—he says with derision:
"You are indeed lovers of substance; you are by no means lovers of quality."
Or rather, it is in an instant that by means of wisdom the person of Śambhu is fashioned. || 42 ||

The point here is this: even when there is a transfer of the qualities of the Supreme Lord, do the impure qualities of the substance perceived as the self still exist at that time, or not? They cannot be said not to exist, because the position that knowledge and action are destroyed will be refuted later. If they do exist, are they, as before, restricted to specific objects or universal in scope?

If they do not have all things as their object, then it has been stated that such a person is merely a beast and is impure. On the other hand, if they have all things as their object through the transference of the qualities of God, then this is simply the purity of the qualities according to our own system; how then can your position—that there is a preference for the purity of the substance of the self alone and a lack of preference for the purity of the qualities—be logically sustained? Furthermore, your derision of the partiality toward qualities shown by the great ones is itself a mockery.

He states another fault for those who maintain the theory of transmigration: "Or [it would be] a moment," and so forth. Furthermore, this has been forgotten by you dualists of Īśvara: that the person, being a transformation of Śambhu, is not imagined [as distinct from Him].
The sense is that, since liberation consists in possessing His qualities, His non-duality is effectively accepted [by you]. || 42 ||
Having thus refuted the position of transmigration (*saṃkrānti*), he now rejects the position of total destruction (*sarvanāśa*):
"An old man would firmly remember the objects perceived during childhood and youth;
consequently, there would be stability for the person throughout the interval between birth and death. (43)
Since it is observed that one is capable of remembering those [experiences] through the recollection of states experienced since childhood,

the stability of the self is accepted on the basis of this observation of memory. For if a different seer were to experience [them] at every moment, then there would be no memory of an object experienced by another.

Otherwise, there would be no [recognition] of "this" as being that, as in the case of Caitra and Maitra. Yet, here we observe the recollection of an object experienced at one time occurring at another time; therefore, stability [of the self] follows. Now, even by you, who maintain that the self is stable, a distinction between experience and recollection must be admitted. For even for you, recollection is not identical to experience, otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of all mental modifications being non-distinct.

Even though those two [the past experience and the present memory] are distinct, you yourself must accept that for an elder person, there is now a memory regarding that past experience—or rather, regarding the object experienced—produced by a mental impression (*citta-saṃskāra*) formed by that past experience; for otherwise, it would follow that the self is subject to modification, since you do not admit the existence of mental impressions. However, between the mental streams of Caitra and Maitra, they are mutually...

Since you have accepted that memory arises through the production of a latent impression (saṃskāra) only from an experience that has fallen within a single stream of consciousness— because there is an absence of any cause for producing a latent impression in anything else— how can non-difference be established here?

If it is argued that non-difference is being proved here for a Self that is distinct from the mental modifications (cittavṛtti), that is incorrect, because [without such a Self] apart from the mental modifications...

Moreover, even if a difference were admitted, the relationship between cause and effect would be undermined.
