Because memory and so forth are established as explained previously. Furthermore, it must be stated: who is the inferrer of that [memory]? It cannot be the mind (*citta*), because it is admitted to be insentient (*acetana*). If it is argued that even though it is insentient, it possesses sentience through contact with that [sentient principle], that is incorrect; for if the insentient becomes sentient through contact with a sentient being, it does not thereby possess the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). If, however, it does possess the nature of consciousness, then it is simply the Self (*ātman*).

What is the point of saying "because of its luminosity"? Nor is it logical for that [object] which is inferred to possess the nature of the Self (*ātman*), because, like the light itself, there is a distinction between the nature of the illuminator and the illuminated. For that which shines by itself is the Self, whereas that which is illuminated by it is its other, the illuminated; thus there is no confusion. Just as in the case of the Self and the other, their natures do not become intermingled, so it is with everything.

Because each [moment of consciousness] is the self of the preceding and succeeding moments; and there is no establishment of the object of illumination (*prakāśya*) upon the establishment of the illumination itself (*prakāśa*), such that one would not admit the illumination of the mind even if the self were imperceptible (*parokṣa*). Thus, total blindness would result for the entire world.
Now, if the illumination of the mind is admitted even when the self is unestablished, then [the mind] is of the nature of illumination.

"Let it be accepted that the mental modification itself, which possesses arising and passing away, is the self; what is the use of establishing the eternity of a self that is distinct from it and absolutely unproven?
[The reply is: It is true that experience is not recollection, and it is true that [recollection arises] from that which has fallen within the same stream [of consciousness].

The arising of memory occurs from the mental impression (*citta-saṃskāra*) produced by the capacity for the functioning of existence and so forth, and not from that which resides in a different stream [of consciousness]. And this is indeed true: namely, the assertion of the non-existence of the self, which is directly perceived by itself, apart from the mind.
For it is not logical for those who deny experience to establish a system based on non-experience. That very [self]...

The establisher [of this] says: "And as for that which is not denied, there is nothing that is not denied; let that very nature which is non-deniable be examined. Does the grasper manifest as a mere momentary appearance, distinct from both the preceding and succeeding moments at every instant, or rather as being always [the same]? Regarding the claim that it is "distinct," this is as follows:

The Light is of a stable nature; it is always such that, even when there is a difference in the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the objects of perception, it does not experience any internal differentiation within itself. Throughout the three periods of time, its prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) and its subsequent destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva) are transcended. Even while there is the cognition of the arising and passing away of various mental modifications through manifold means of knowledge, it remains one as the witness of their stability, its own luminosity undiminished even amidst other mental states.

Even in states such as deep sleep, one's own consciousness remains unbroken; because it is always cognizable through its own self-luminosity, that which is denoted by the term "Self" is established for every person through their own direct experience. What need is there for any other means of proof here? It is precisely by relying upon this very self-consciousness—undivided and imperishable—that all people undertake actions whose fruits are realized at a later time. For if that consciousness were momentary, [such action would be impossible].

Since all worldly transactions cease—because every cognition perishes immediately after being experienced for a mere moment and cannot possibly arise again in the subsequent moment—who would engage in activity, where, or for what purpose? For one who maintains the doctrine of momentariness and perceives neither "I" nor "mine," no engagement is possible; thus, there remains only a desireless, self-abiding, pure luminosity.
The world would be devoid of the cognition of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, and empty of various cognitions such as the investigation and understanding of false knowledge;
for all this [including] pleasure and so forth, is preceded by a stable illuminating subject. Thus, this illumination, which serves as the cause of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), is undeniable.
The cause for the production of a fruit that arises at a later time would have to exist at all times.

True; this grasper too is of a single form, a stable luminosity of the grasper, capable of accomplishing all worldly transactions, and indeed undeniable. However, it is not self-cognizable, but rather...

When only the stream of moments of the subject (*grāhakakṣaṇapravāha*) is being experienced, it is superimposed and manifested by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) through the delusion of perceiving similarity to that [preceding moment]. Therefore, it is not merely an error that the stream itself possesses unity; rather, because its unity is cognized as an object (*karmatayā*) due to the distinctness of the [apprehended] objects. For if this were indeed a superimposition, then that which is intended as the superimposer would, by its own nature, exist for only a single moment.

Because [the object] does not appear as something that has perished; for if it were to appear as such, its nature as the self (ātmatva) would be established. Furthermore, since superimposition consists in the reflective awareness of a prior and a subsequent state, it must be removable by a stable cognition. Nor can even a momentary cognition be a locus of superimposition, because it cannot simultaneously possess a long-range object characterized by both the prior and the subsequent.

Because it lacks conceptual construction (*avikalpaka*) by virtue of not consisting of a synthesis (*ayojanātmakatva*), it is like the appearance of a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*) and so forth. For this very reason, it has been stated that even though the cognition of a yogi has all objects as its domain simultaneously, it is considered non-conceptual. If it is argued that "its objects are synthesized," this is of no consequence, because synthesis is impossible since all things are momentary (*kṣaṇika*). Therefore, even for multiple moments of conceptualization that occur sequentially...

It is not a state of superimposition (*āropaka*), because superimposition is impossible due to the absence of conceptualization (*vikalpana*) regarding its constituent parts. Nor can it be said to reside within the very nature of the subject (*grāhaka*), such that the conceptual construction would be non-conceptual with respect to itself. For this very reason, even its status as the object of the "I-notion" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) is impossible; rather, it consists precisely in the luminous nature of the manifestation of the "I-notion," since even then the "I" appears as stable in that very form. Indeed, not...

It has been stated that the destruction of the subject-self is perceived even throughout the three periods of time. For whatever has prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), that has arisen; and for whatever person there is an arising, he is [subsequently] destroyed. However, the "I-notion" (ahaṃpratyaya) has no non-existence at either the prior or subsequent limits [of time]. Consciousness (saṃvit) arises at every moment.

It cannot be said that [the quality] has become firmly established (*nirūḍhā*), nor will we say that it is a property of consciousness that is self-cognized (*svasaṃvedya*). Because stability and momentariness are mutually contradictory in form—just as grossness and subtlety are—the momentariness of lightning and such things, being established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-siddha*), excludes non-momentariness. Just so it is here.

It is logical that the appearance of stability, which arises through the impossibility of superimposing [the nature of] another upon itself, excludes momentariness without doubt. Furthermore, sublation of self-cognition is not possible, by virtue of which it might become erroneous, as we shall explain later. Nor does the acceptance of something established by a means of valid cognition in a manner other than it actually is—absent a sublater—convince the minds of the wise.

If it is argued that the impossibility of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) for a permanent entity is itself the subverting proof, we say no; for since that impossibility will be refuted therein, it lacks the power to subvert [our position]. Thus, in this *Prakāśa*, with respect to the Self—which is the witness of the arising and passing away of one's own mind, which is of a permanent nature, and which is the grasper—it has been stated that its agency is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). This results in the manifestation of self-consciousness, which serves as the means to refute the arguments put forward by others regarding its non-existence.

It is produced by causes through a lateral succession of causal factors, and not by memory; for that [memory] is indeed distinct from the past experience. However, the rememberer does not differ, because he is experienced as the very same prior experiencer at that time through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Thus, due to this non-difference, there is a metaphorical designation of non-difference there, but in reality there is no non-difference. Enough, then, with this analysis of extremely subtle experience, which only causes mental exhaustion for ascetics of dull intellect.

Having thus established the stability of the person between birth and death, he now says— [in order] to prove [the existence of the self] prior to birth, against those who claim that knowledge arises from the elements alone—
that the memory of an object experienced in another birth could not possibly belong to anyone else.
And that [craving] becomes hunger because of its tendency to move toward breast milk. || 44 ||

For if consciousness were to arise together with the body, then a newborn infant on that very day, when hungry, would have no inclination toward food— that is, no activity consisting of swallowing— for the sake of obtaining milk.

This is an illustration [of the process], including other factors such as the placement of the articulatory organs (*sthāna*), the effort of the organs (*karaṇa*), and their impact (*abhighāta*). As they say: "The initial arrangement of the organs, the upward movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the impact upon the points of articulation do not occur without prior cognition—that is, without the cultivation of sound" (*Vākyapadīya* 1.114). And this is indeed observed.

[This] activity [is observed]; it indicates at that time a memory preceded by another birth. But is it not the case that just as the emergence of yawning and so forth in an infant occurs through the power of things alone, by virtue of the nature of the species (*jāti-dharma*), so too will this [activity] be? This is incorrect. For all of this is preceded by comprehension; indeed, there is no emergence without comprehension, unlike [the growth of] hair, nails, and the like.

It is logical that yawning and the like are properties of a genus (*jāti-dharmatā*), because they occur spontaneously. However, the swallowing of milk is not a property of a genus, because it is observed to be accomplished by a specific effort produced by desire; for even an infant born at that very moment draws milk from the breast with a specific effort due to its need, and having drawn it in, he fills his mouth and does not vomit it, but rather—

Even while swallowing, he is seen swallowing in such a manner that the limit of the fruit characterized by satiety is reached; and as the obstruction of the vital air (prāṇa) arises for him in this way, because one observes the performance of specific efforts caused by the acquisition of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful, the proof of the recollection of previously experienced benefit and harm—inferred from knowing the children's notions of what is beneficial and what is harmful—is established. || 44 ||
On this very point, he states the following argument:
"People who possess the memory of their past lives (*jātismara*) are observed providing proof;
yet, a memory of an object experienced by one person cannot possibly belong to another. (45)

Those who remember their past lives, the *jātismaras*, are indeed directly perceived. If it is argued that memory regarding another birth has been seen or inferred, he asks: "What follows from that? He replies: "And not by another. It has already been established that experience and memory share a single substratum; therefore, this is true even prior to birth.
The existence of the experiencer is established. || 45 ||
Then, [the author] asks: "What follows from this established fact?
and says: "In this way, the beginningless sequence of births of persons must be inferred;
for the measurement of a beginningless entity would not be possible if it were subject to destruction. (46)

Because one observes that every birth is preceded by the habitual tendencies (*saṃskāra*) and prior conduct from previous births, the continuity of birth for a person is established; thus, their beginninglessness is proven. It is not, however, the case that they are produced from the primary elements (*bhūta*) alone.

Therefore, since beginninglessness is established, the position of universal destruction is refuted; thus he says "of that which is beginningless," and so forth. [This applies] to the state of being perishable.

For a thing that is beginningless (*anādi*), there can be no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its perishability; since there is an absence of a means of valid cognition, the impossibility of its destruction is indicated. Therefore, the meaning is that the perishability of a beginningless thing is not conceivable. For impermanence is established for things possessing origination because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established, but not for things lacking origination; hence, it is one whose nature is non-origination (*anutpattidharman*).
And it has been stated that [the self] exists.

This might be the case: there is a proof for the perishability of the beginningless self, namely its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). For instance, the performance of causal efficiency is the very nature of a permanent entity; because if it lacked this, the consequence would be its non-existence as a real thing (*avastutva*). And that—

Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is indeed one; for if it possessed a manifold intrinsic nature, it too would be manifold, since the definition of the difference between entities is the difference in their intrinsic natures. Furthermore, if the difference between entities were to consist in a single intrinsic nature, then because that nature would always possess the capacity to perform all causal functions through its own manifestation, there would follow the consequence that even in a single moment it would perform all its effects simultaneously, due to the simultaneity of those effects resulting from that very nature.
Even then, because [the cause] exists, there would be no sequential production of effects.
Furthermore, there would be no restriction regarding the time of the action. If it possessed that same nature in the second moment as well, it would act in exactly the same way.

It would perform in the first moment alone those purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*) performed in the second moment, and conversely, it would perform in the second moment those actions performed in the first moment.

Because of such instability, it is impossible for a single nature to produce effects even simultaneously; thus, that [instability], being untenable there, finds its rest in the absence of other modes—namely, in non-existences that perish in a mere moment—as a property of things that are the opposite of that [stability]. Therefore, things are momentary. For if they were momentary, that [nature] would be the performer of the preceding causal efficiency.

Another [entity] is destroyed, and a new one arises as an unprecedented performer of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever regarding purposeful action being experienced sequentially; therefore, there is no fault. Consequently, for the self (*ātman*) as well, its very definition as purposeful action is the proof of its perishability; thus, it is established that the self is perishable.

This is incorrect, because the cognizer, which is one's own self, is experienced precisely as being stable. Nor is it correct to say that even the analysis of moments—such as the cessation of intrinsic nature—is impossible here [in the case of the self] if it were momentary; for that too is untenable. Furthermore, one should not claim that stability will arise from something constructed by illusion, because there is no error in self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*). And therefore:

The appearance of stability in the apprehending subject, along with the self-corroborating evidence provided by the inference of identity—which is characterized by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the observations of deliberation—constitutes the valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) that sublates momentariness as defined by the impossibility of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Now, it was argued that causal efficiency is not possible for a stable entity; however, that too is incorrect, because even if that entity possesses a single nature, [causal efficiency occurs] when specific auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*) are present.

Because its very nature consists solely in the production of the effect, it produces [the effect] only when those [auxiliaries] are present, and not before, due to their absence; thus, there is no impossibility of the effect occurring sequentially. Now, as for a seed situated in a granary, whether or not it possesses the capacity to produce a sprout when the auxiliary causes such as soil are present—whether that capacity exists or does not exist.

Whether it be the cooperative factor itself or the capacity to produce that effect, since its nature is exclusively to produce the effect when the cooperative factors are present, it lacks that capacity when they are absent due to having a single nature.

Alternatively, if the capacity is acquired from the cooperative factors, then it was previously incapable and later becomes capable; thus, because of this difference in nature, there is indeed a distinction [in the entity] itself, and not oneness.
To this it is replied: although capable, this [cause] produces the effect only when that [auxiliary] is present, because its nature is such;
it does not do so at other times. [Objection: If it is capable, why does it depend on presence? [Reply:
It has already been stated that it is because its nature is such. By its own causes, or by its very nature, that entity arises as possessing precisely such a nature.

When something that is capable produces an effect only when certain auxiliary causes (sahakārikāraṇa) are present, and not otherwise, positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) serve as the means of valid cognition regarding a stable entity. Furthermore, the intrinsic natures (svabhāva) of things do not admit of questioning;
for it is impossible to raise the question, "Why does fire burn and not water? This remains true even when the auxiliary causes are present.

If it is argued that its nature is distinct from the producer simply because of the absence of production, even then there is no difference, because its nature is solely the performance of the effect upon the presence of auxiliary causes; for when those are present, it is indeed that same [nature]. Indeed, an entity never deviates from this nature throughout the three periods of time. However, due to the non-presence of auxiliary causes, the effect does not arise at that time.
Thus, it is only the presence and absence of that [auxiliary] which differ, but there is no difference in the entity itself.

Now, if presence and absence reside in the auxiliary, then the two auxiliaries would produce a distinction [in the effect], because they possess contradictory natures. There is no contradiction even in that case, for that [distinction] is also produced by the presence [of the cause] in the auxiliary. Regarding that auxiliary...

Because its nature is one of proximity (*sannidhi-svabhāvatva*), it too [produces its effect] when other auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) are present; thus, there is no lack of regularity. Since the diversity of entities is determined by their inherent natures (*svabhāva-niyama*), even for auxiliary causes such as soil and the like, when they are in proximity to a cause such as a seed, their capacity to produce that effect is precisely that very similar nature (*tatsadṛśa eva svabhāvaḥ*) by which the effect occurs only upon their presence.

Since nothing else occurs while [the action] is being performed, the nature of being a causal factor (*kāraka*) for all [factors] depends upon their mutual proximity; thus, all causal factors are designated as "cooperative" (*sahakārin*), and not each one individually. Nor is there a difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). And although all possess efficacy, there is no contingency of multiple effects arising, because [they act] only in mutual proximity.
Because its nature is to accomplish that single effect, even when performing various successive causal operations in the presence of various auxiliary factors,
it remains a single entity whose nature is to produce those various multiple effects in succession.

There is no difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*). For example, in the case of a single person such as Caitra, who performs various functions like cutting, cooking, and eating, although there is a sequence of actions such as cutting, there is no difference in his intrinsic nature; because when the respective auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*) such as a sickle are present, he possesses the intrinsic nature of performing those specific actions like cutting, and it is precisely that kind of intrinsic nature which exists therein in a sequential manner.

For you yourselves have accepted that a single lamp possesses a single nature capable of accomplishing multiple functions—such as burning the wick, consuming the oil, and illuminating itself—yet there is no difference in its nature due to the difference in these effects.
This is because there is no contradiction in a single, specific nature producing multiple effects; the same should be accepted in this case as well.

Because a stable entity is never dissociated from its nature of performing various distinct effects when the respective auxiliary conditions (sahakārin) are present, and because the presence of those auxiliaries—just as before—is sequential, it is possible for that stable entity to accomplish multiple effects in succession. Thus, even though the entity is not diverse in its nature, there is no contradiction in its being a performer of purposeful action (arthakriyā) through successive stages; therefore, the occurrence of purposeful action is indeed possible here.

This constitutes a sublation, because such [sublation] is possible regarding stable entities. Furthermore, how causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is impossible for that which is momentary has been analyzed by us in the *Āgamaviveka*; therefore, it should be understood from that very source.
Since there is no such sublation in that case, the stability of entities is established by perception and is indeed uncontradicted.

In this regard, their cause is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Those [entities] are perishable, whereas others are indeed imperishable; thus, even though the self performs purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), its imperishability is established due to the absence of a cause [for its destruction].

By this, the previously mentioned contradiction regarding the self's nature as a knower (*jñatva*) is also resolved, because—just as before—it possesses a single nature that grasps each respective object upon the proximity of those various objects.

Because there is no difference in their essential nature (*bhāva*), the delusion regarding their contradiction due to a perceived difference in nature—arising from a mistaken cognition of that nature prior to the apprehension of the jar—is thus refuted. Consequently, since the subject (*grāhaka*) is indestructible and the object (*grāhya*) as a substantial entity does not exist, there is no destruction of these two in liberation; rather, omniscience alone is logical. [This applies] to those whose nature is obscuration (*āvṛti*).
Because ignorance and the other afflictions—known as impurity, karma, and illusion—have at that time ceased, the grasper remains unobscured.
As they have said: "This mind is luminous by nature; the stains are adventitious. In their absence, it is the imperishable light for all objects. (46)

Having thus refuted the position that everything is annihilated, he now speaks in order to reject the position that the agency of knowledge is destroyed: "Nor is there a destruction of the act of knowing, because that would contradict all the scriptures; furthermore, there is a logical sublation regarding the existence of the Lord, since both [knowledge and agency] are observed to be eternal. (47)

This position, which denies the existence of knowledge and action in liberation, is refuted by the scriptural text: "For there is no loss of the vision of the seer, nor of the thought of the thinker" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23). Furthermore, it is not appropriate to accept a reality that contradicts all the scriptures, as they say:
"But the intuition of the one who has reached the end of doubt is distinguished. Now, even if an object exists, those who are stainless do not [perceive it]...

They claim that by the power of reasoning, [the opponents] perceive [this] and thereby lead one to accept even a reality contrary to that [scriptural view]. To this, he replies: "He is the Lord who exists" (*sadīśa*).

He is both "existent" (*sat*) because he is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and "Lord" (*īśvara*). Since the eternality of knowledge and action is observed in Him, this position is sublated by the aforementioned inference. The meaning is as follows: for the proponent of the compendium of categories (*padārthasaṃgrahavādin*), the Lord is first of all a "substance" (*dravya*) category.

Thus, even in that case, its inclusion must be stated as being within the category of the self (*ātman*) alone and not elsewhere, because it is utterly dissimilar [to other categories] and therefore cannot be joined with them.

For if it were not included therein, it would either constitute a separate category (*padārtha*) or a separate substance (*dravya*), which would contradict the accepted doctrine that there are six categories or nine substances. Let it be that it is included therein.

What follows from this? Furthermore, by means of the following reasoning, the position that knowledge and action are destroyed [in liberation] is also refuted: "The liberated selves, being subjects of disagreement [with the opponent], are omniscient and all-powerful, because, while possessing the nature of a self, they are devoid of merit and demerit, just like the Lord (Īśvara).
For indeed, the absence of merit and demerit is established through their omniscience and all-powerfulness.

Since it is established that [the power] pervading the Lord manifests those respective forms for those whose nature is Being, all liberated ones thus become equal to the Lord; therefore, it is not logical that there should be a destruction of the agency of knowledge and action in liberation. || 47 ||
Now, with the verse beginning "Regarding the indeterminate [states], etc. (Śloka 2), he refutes the positions previously mentioned:
"Because there is a return for those who are dissolved in the *upādānas*, they have fallen into dissolution while being utterly deluded regarding the domain of the causal principle. (48)

Granted that liberation (mokṣa) would consist in the dissolution of individual souls— being effects— into that Supreme Being who is the non-effectual Self and is designated as the Great Glory, just as jars and other objects dissolve into clay; however, the meaning is that from that state,
upon the commencement of creation following the dissolution, there would be for them a returning, a revolving, and a falling back into saṃsāra.

He states the reason with the words "yataḥ" (since). The "authority" (*adhikāra*) of the cause consists in its capacity for transformation back into the form of the effect, precisely because it possesses the nature of modification (*pariṇāma*); for it is by means of that [nature] that the cause is exercised in that form. Since [the souls] are merged within such a cause, they would, upon liberation, undergo transformation again through a return [to worldly existence], just like bound souls; thus, in this context, the purpose of liberation would be futile.

"The effort [is for those who maintain] its dissolution" means this: it might be argued that although at the time of dissolution all individual souls (jīvātman)—both bound and unbound—are dissolved therein, nevertheless, at the time of re-creation, he returns as a bound soul alone, endowed with the latent impressions (vāsanā) of ignorance (avidyā) and so forth, and not as an unbound one, because the causes of return, such as ignorance, are absent there. That is incorrect, because of that—

In that state, because there is no division, the state of non-division itself constitutes causality. Even there, since a division between the bound and the unbound is preceded by a prior state of non-division, the inference of its primal cause (*prakṛti*) is quite clear;
therefore, that *prakṛti* is not "higher," because another *prakṛti* exists beyond it. Regarding that other *prakṛti*:
Furthermore, since the objections and their refutations have already been stated, there would be an infinite regress; thus, [the self] is of an undivided nature.

Even if it is of an undivided nature, because the supreme cause exists as such even prior [to creation], its essential nature is immeasurable, and therefore no increase is possible for it even upon the dissolution of the individual soul (jīvātman), especially since the individual soul is not perceived therein. If, at best, that individual soul...

An entity previously perceived as performing purposeful action, if not perceived in its own nature [later], must be considered simply destroyed; thus, self-annihilation would necessarily follow in liberation. He will state that this is another fault of his position: "Those for whom their own self perishes are the foremost among the foolish" (verse 57). However, the non-occurrence of the aforementioned faults does not follow merely from this.

It might be argued: "What can we do? Since this consequence follows from valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), by whom can it be averted? To this he says: "They are perverted" (*viparyastā*). It is not as if that [consequence] were merely based on valid means of knowledge; rather, here the "impurity" (*mala*) is perversion, which is false cognition (*mithyājñāna*). For instance, it is not logical for two effects that are contrary to consciousness to arise from a single material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) whose nature is consciousness.

Because two contradictory things cannot have a single substratum, just as existence and non-existence cannot; furthermore, because its modifications partake of both the conditions and the non-conditions of consciousness, the ultimate cause itself would have to be both conscious and unconscious in nature. And this, like the barrenness of a mother, cannot be established even by Brahmā himself. Now, suppose someone were to claim that it has a certain part...

It is said that no one is conscious. If this is so, then since [the self] is not established as an effect by virtue of its generic similarity (*sabhāgatva*)—just like a jar—the aforementioned defect remains as it was. Furthermore, if the state of being an effect were established for individual souls (*jīvātman*), then its cause would be established as the supreme *prakṛti*;

however, because those souls are themselves conscious, they cannot be effects. As for the claim that their state of being an effect follows from positive concomitance (*anvaya*), that too is incorrect.

Because the possession (*samanvaya*) of selves is already established. For possession is logically possible only for that which is to be grasped when it has attained the state of being an object (*karman*). And a self cannot be the object of its own self, because its own operation upon itself is a contradiction.
Indeed, it was stated previously that it always appears as the subject (*grāhaka*), by virtue of its nature as the immediate witness.

It might be argued as follows: "The connection with the apprehended object (*grāhya-samanvaya*) is grasped only by one who has become the apprehended; however, the connection with the apprehending subject (*grāhaka-samanvaya*) appears within that very self (*ātman*) when it appears in its nature as the apprehender. To this, the reply is: "Indeed, the connection with an apprehender is preceded by the manifestation of multiple apprehenders; and there is no self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) of an apprehender whose essential nature is a single self."

There is the cognition of another cognizer, because that [other cognizer] is distinct from him, like a jar or other objects; for selves are not described as being mutually cognizable merely by their own self-cognition, since that would entail the consequence of omniscience at all times. If each [self] were cognized only within its own self, what could have anvaya (logical concomitance) with what? If this were so, then all selves would be [objects] for the omniscient one.

[The opponent argues: "Since they do not transcend the state of being objects of apprehension (*grāhyatva*), all of them will indeed grasp the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) among those very things that are non-apprehensible. This is incorrect, because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the omniscient self itself. For even he, by means of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), appears as the subject of this [cognition] in his non-difference from the supreme selves. And it has been stated that a positive concomitance is not possible for that which is not apprehended; nor is that [omniscient self] [non-apprehensible], because of his omniscience.
A mistaken apprehension is thus established.

For example: by means of his own experience, which is itself an error, he has grasped his own self as being of a nature entirely non-concomitant with other selves, because [such a thing] is impossible; and in the very same way, he has grasped other selves as being mutually distinct.

There is no fault, for those [objects] which exist beyond the state of being objects of concomitance (*samanvaya*) are directly realized by that [consciousness]. For this very reason, it is not an object of inference; for the selves of others do not appear with a dissimilarity such as that of the mother [to the child], but rather they appear as utterly dissimilar even to one's own self, and thus cannot be inferred. If this were so, the Self would be non-existent, like a horse’s horn.

"Because they are not connected with [the universal] existence (sattā)"—it is not because of a connection with existence that the selves (ātman) possess existence here; rather, they possess existence by virtue of their own essential nature (svarūpasattva), like existence itself or like the supreme cause (paramakāraṇa). For even in the case of that [supreme cause], you must not maintain that its existence arises from a connection with existence, as that would entail the consequence of it being an effect (kāryatva). Rather, its very essence is existence itself; thus, it is not equivalent to a horse's horn. How so?

In the absence of a common lineage (*anvaya*) for those [non-selves], the manifestation of the single term "existent" (*sat*) for all non-selves constitutes the attainment of the status of a self. Furthermore, if it is asked how even that [status] can be investigated regarding selves, then what attachment would there be for a clever person to insist on the provision of a common lineage of existence?
Moreover, the application of a single term everywhere is not based solely upon a single common lineage, as is the case with words such as "tree," which possess multiple forms.

Furthermore, since usage is observed even when [the term] is not denotative [of a genus], there is no fault here, as it is possible for words such as "cook" (*pācaka*) to function through the force of their etymological derivation (*yoga*). Alternatively, even if a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is impossible as stated, the application of a single word to individual selves is based solely on similarity, just as the word "jar" applies to various jars. Thus...
Because that which consists of a specific configuration is denoted by the word "jar," and because that [configuration] is no different even in another jar.

Now, it might be argued that there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) among jars by virtue of their being "jarness" (*ghaṭatva*). If this were so, it would follow that the production of jars arises from jarness due to that concomitance. However, jars do not arise from jarness; rather, they arise from clay.

Therefore, similarity is one thing and positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is another. For here, "similarity" is said to be the universal (*sāmānya*), which is the cause for [a cognition] being expressed by a single word, as in: "This too is a jar; that too is a jar. And that [universal] does not reside in its parts. For the cognition of a "jar" does not occur in the neck or the base, nor is it seen in its effects such as potsherds and the like; [for] among potsherds...

This is because [the cognition] has the jar as its object precisely through its dissimilarity [to other things]. However, that entity whose effect persists in every respect—even in an object that is more similar to it part by part—in that very form, is called "concomitance" (*anvaya*). And that alone serves as the basis for postulating a single cause.
For this is observed in the case of jars, shards, and so forth, even though they are highly dissimilar, yet their constituent parts persist.

The distinction is this: since clay is observed to persist in all its effects, such as the neck and so forth, as well as in the potsherds and so forth, the invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) with being an effect of clay is established.

As for similarity and persistence, even though they do not persist elsewhere [in the same substratum], the application of a single term based on similarity alone is possible; thus there is no fault. For this very reason, the author of the Vṛtti says therein: "Śiva is of the same genus as the Self."
"The very similarity [of cognitions] is their existence here.
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that even this similarity cannot be grasped, since its nature is ungraspable? True;

however, just as [the term] 'self' (ātman) is used as a designation despite being ungraspable, so too—in order to facilitate conventional usage—is there the mere indication of dissimilarity by way of a slight proximity [to the graspable].
This is metaphorically applied here, not in reality; as they say: "The realization of the Self is 'not this, not this'. Thus, everything is faultless.

And so, even though there exists a supreme cause consisting of conscious material (upādāna), the defect of repeated return has been stated with regard to liberation, which consists of attaining that [cause]. By this very [reasoning], others [are also refuted].

Those who maintain the doctrine of the dissolution of the vital breaths, the ego, and so forth, as previously mentioned, have been refuted—on the grounds that there would be a return for those dissolved into their respective material causes (upādāna). || 48 ||

Now, he refutes the position that "dissolution occurs in the Supreme Self" (verse 2): "The status of the Supreme Self as the material cause is well-established in the Vedānta; for that which is dissolved into its material cause, there is certainly a re-emergence, just as before. (49)

That the Supreme Self is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the entire universe is indeed well-known in the Vedāntic scriptures. The meaning is that for those who are merged or seated within that material cause, there must necessarily be a cessation from its nature and a subsequent return, just as before. Now, according to the previously presented Vedāntic perspective, this entire world consisting of duality—
It is argued that since [the world] is unreal due to being a manifestation of ignorance (*avidyā*), it cannot be an effect; how then can Brahman be its material cause?

In this regard, the fault is apprehended as follows: How is that world unreal? Or what is defined as real? To this they reply: The very nature of consciousness (*bodha*) is the definition of reality. Due to the absence of that [consciousness], [the world is unreal].

The unreality of jars and the like [is established] because those cognitions do not consist of the object of cognition. As they have said: "For that which has no cognition by another, a distinction between existence and non-existence based on mere variety is appropriate for the wise, since the opposite is also possible. However, if it were non-existent, a reason for its being existent must be stated as a non-sublater; without a sublater," [the status of existence remains].
The existence of all entities is established by experience, and it is not proper for those who possess discernment to abandon it.

It might be argued as follows: since objects cognizable by others cannot be analyzed—either as being composed of atoms or as having a gross nature—they are non-entities; like dreams, they consist of ignorance and are incapable of being defined by themselves.
Or rather, the very nature of ignorance is its incapacity for self-definition, whereas the nature of knowledge is precisely its capacity for self-definition;
since the reality whose essence is consciousness is established by itself as having that single nature and thus acts as its own regulator, it does not possess such [incapacity].
Therefore, this [incapacity] is the cause of non-existence and the subverter of existence.
In this regard, the investigation is as follows: *pratibhā* is a specific means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arising from the intuition of a person.

Now, if the person’s means of valid cognition is characterized by an inability to determine the true nature of things due to being overcome by ignorance and epilepsy, and due to a deficiency in intuition—well, what fault have the objects committed that they should be rendered non-existent by such [a person]?
These are said to be non-existent. For it is not the fault of the post that the blind man does not see it; rather, it is the fault of the person.

And because entities are impossible to investigate [in their ultimate nature], doubt regarding them is appropriate, since such doubt is logically established by the absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to either prove or refute them. It is not, however, a certainty of their non-existence.

The investigation of those [entities] has been properly undertaken through the analysis of the intrinsic nature of things (*bhāvasvabhāva*), because doubt regarding them has been thus established even among cowherds, women, children, and the elderly. Nor is it the case that entities are incapable of being investigated, since this was already investigated in detail previously in the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*); therefore, their unreality does not follow from this either.

But was it not stated previously that Brahman alone is real, while the distinctions are unreal? Since the Veda possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) even by virtue of establishing established facts (*siddhārtha*), the distinction between the real and the unreal is determined by the Veda. If this is so, then because the Vedic statements here also possess the status of valid knowledge, they too would be real; thus, there would be a contradiction with non-duality (*advaita*), which holds that Brahman alone is real.

Because non-duality is based upon the existence of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and so forth. Now, if it is maintained that even these Vedic statements are themselves unreal, then, being invalid, another means of knowledge must be stated for the sake of establishing the reality of Brahman and the unreality of duality through them. For an unreal statement cannot serve as a means of knowledge, like the cognition of the son of a barren woman; therefore, [another] means of knowledge...

Since the objections and their rebuttals are exactly as stated previously, there is no finality; thus, the establishment of the reality of non-duality (*advaita*) does not occur. If, in ultimate reality, difference (*bheda*) truly exists, then how can those [cognitions] have non-duality as their very nature? For whom and with respect to what would they be means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), given that they are based upon duality?

Regarding the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of cognition (*prameya*): if you argue that this is true insofar as, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), this entire convention of means of cognition and so forth is merely of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*), we reply: surely that very point is what is being investigated!

Since the means of cognition are unreal, even this certainty of yours is not a valid cognition (*apramā*). Furthermore, whatever has been understood by you is indeed unreal, like the appearance of two moons and the like.

Since even Brahman is unreal, the total non-existence of everything has been correctly established by those possessed of wisdom. [Objection: But surely even the Vedic statements, though consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*), serve as the very means for attaining knowledge (*vidyā*). [Reply: This is a deceptive statement intended to delude ignorant Vedic scholars. If the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are unreal, then all of this is like a mere daydream. If they are real, [then...]

Or rather, it is only the dualistic position that appears [as real]. For if there were non-difference from That, then "all this is indeed Brahman," and in that case, it would be incoherent to ask who could do what to whom. In that state, no delusion is possible for the original object (*bimba*). Even delusion—such as the cognition of dreams and the like—takes everything as its objective support (*ālambana*), yet the deluded one does not [delude] himself. And the objective support is something existing externally, appearing otherwise.
It renders [the object] an object of delusion. However, that entity whose very nature is pure consciousness exists exactly as it is;

for it is impossible for that which is self-cognized to possess a different nature from that [consciousness]. Or, if it did possess that nature, it would be nothing other than self-cognized; thus, since delusion is impossible within self-cognition, the distinction between selves is established by self-cognition through each person’s status as an inferer of another's self.
It is indeed true. Scripture also says: "Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.15; Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.14; Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.10).

Now, an objection may be raised: since difference depends upon the establishment of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), and since perception has positive entities as its object, how [can it apprehend difference]?
Is difference perceived directly? As it has been said: "They say that perception is affirmative" (*Brahmasiddhi* 2.1).
Difference and unity do not depend on the establishment of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*). Rather, once difference is established, there is the cognition of that mutual non-existence.
For if everything were one, nothing would be absent from anything; thus, why would one seeking a jar turn away upon seeing a cloth? [This is] by means of the instrument of knowledge...

Furthermore, there would be no distinction between the means of valid cognition and their objects, because [the object] would never deviate from mere existence (*sattāmātra*). Since the difference among all cognitions is established through non-perception (*apratyakṣasiddha*), how can its unreality be proven by mere recitation? Let it be real; nevertheless, since scripture states that this [world] has Brahman as its material cause (*upādāna*), Brahman will be its material cause. If that is so, then this very point has been stated here.

The author of the commentary [asks]: "For what purpose is this objection? [It is] because those who are dissolved in the material causes (upādāna) undergo rebirth. He states the answer—pointing out that the fault mentioned here has already been addressed—in the verse beginning with "upādāna" (verse 49).

But is it not heard in scripture that bliss (*ānanda*) is the form of Brahman? And since there can be no reversal from that form, even if the gross form is reversed, the defect of reversal will not apply to those who have merged into it. To this he says:
"Bliss is merely consciousness; the reality is true, for there is no [reversal] therein."
The wise have never observed such a material cause as threads and the like [to be produced by themselves].

O wise ones, O scholars! In that Brahman, there is no cognition in the ultimate sense, because it is the material cause [of all], just as threads and so forth are the material causes of cloth and other such things. || 50 ||
How, then, are these scriptural passages to be understood? He says:
"For one who has entered into the state of being a world-being and remains therein, there is established, according to their qualities, the primary characteristic of those enjoyers who reside there."

That Brahman, having transformed itself as the bestower of experience (bhoga), possesses the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*) which serves as the cause of the world; this is stated figuratively (*guṇata upacārataḥ*) on account of its connection with the consciousness of the experiencers residing in the world, but not in a primary sense. The meaning is that the scriptural passages stating "consciousness is the form of Brahman" are to be explained through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), just as one says, "the platforms are shouting. As they say:
Regarding the word "there" (tatra): in that context, this is the primary form of the selves of the enjoyers residing in the worlds, and not that of Brahmā. || 51 ||
To the objection that liberation for us will then consist in attaining such a world, he says:
"Because the destructibility of the world is observed, upon its destruction, there would also be the destruction of those who enjoy it; therefore, this is not an eternal state. (52)
Since the destruction of the enjoyer is observed upon the destruction of the world, that liberation (mokṣa) is also impermanent. || 52 ||
Having thus rejected the position of absorption into the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), he now refutes liberation as absolute isolation (*kaivalya*):
"Because no karma remains to be experienced beyond the level of the *guṇas*."
Even the liberation (kaivalya) of the Sāṃkhyas is not at all logical, because [the afflictions] are not subject to destruction.

The isolation (*kaivalya*) of the Sāṃkhyas, which consists in the cessation of being an enjoyer through the destruction of karma upon liberation, is untenable. Why? To this he says: "because of non-destruction. The connection is with "of the karma that is to be experienced beyond the *guṇa*-principles. Even though the enjoyment of the *guṇas* has ceased for those liberated according to Sāṃkhya, nevertheless, [there remains] above the *guṇa*-principles... [the Sāṃkhya-aparigaṇita...].

Since the karmas whose objects are the principles such as passion (rāga) and ignorance (avidyā) have not been exhausted, the state of being their experiencer has certainly not ceased. To the question, "How is it that those karmas do not undergo destruction at that time? he says: "Because of non-perception" (anupalabdhitah). Perception (upalabdhi) is experience (bhoga), as it has been stated:
"Experience for this person is sensation" (vedanā). The absence of that is non-perception. Therefore, [the exhaustion occurs] gradually, step by step.

The meaning is that those actions, which have as their object the established reality (*sthitatattva*), must be experienced; they have not yet been exhausted by experience. Now, one might object: "O Arjuna, the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes" (Bhagavad Gītā 4.37).
Since the fruit of Sāṃkhya knowledge is merely the discernment (*viveka*) between the qualities (*guṇa*) and the Puruṣa, how can it be said that those actions are not destroyed?

If that is the knowledge of Sāṃkhya, then what occasion is there for the destruction of karma following it? [Objection: But surely, since the instruments such as the intellect (*buddhi*) also cease upon the cessation of the *guṇas*, how can there be experience without those instruments? [Reply: The activity of the *guṇas* is not the cause of the connection between the self and the instruments; rather, it is the *karmas*, provided that there is equilibrium (*sāmya*). As it has been said: "And bodies arise from karma."

"Objects and causes" (Svāyambhuva 32.13). Thus, since actions have been mentioned, they exist for them; therefore, because the causes [of bondage] have not ceased, there arises the doubt regarding their state as enjoyers: "Is it absolute isolation? What then? Is it through Sāṃkhya knowledge that these [causes] cease? What else could be brought to an end? It is precisely the cessation of being an enjoyer of the *guṇas*. || 53 ||

In this regard, from the perspective of a particular Sāṃkhya school, the opponent demonstrates the exhaustion of all karma through experience: "Not every single action that produces a birth [is exhausted] by that experience, because of the scriptural teaching on the dissolution of the substrate;
even in the Veda, the fruits such as the status of Indra are said to be distinct for each. (54)
Whatever collection of auspicious and inauspicious karma has been performed here between birth and departure, all of that—
existing in the relationship of primary and secondary factors and manifested at the time of departure— produces simultaneously and entirely a single birth;
it does not remain or wait to yield its fruit in another birth, because it exists in the form of action.

The proponents of the doctrine of a single birth (*ekabhavika-karmavādin*) maintain that it is impossible for karma whose effects have already begun to manifest to cease. Consequently, they infer that the exhaustion of all their prior karmas occurs through this very current birth, while the exhaustion of newly acquired karma is brought about by knowledge (*jñāna*) and other means. They further hold that the stream of karma to be experienced in the realms above the *guṇatattva* arises from that [birth]. He refutes this, saying "No; this is not so."

This is a restrictive rule; however, there are certain actions that become the agents of a second or subsequent birth. Why is this so? He says: "In the material cause. For it is heard in scripture that the dissolution of actions occurs in the material cause (*prakṛti*) as their persistence in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). Thus, all [actions] remain in the material cause as karmic impressions. Then, having reached the time for their ripening, they proceed again toward experience.

Thus [it is said]. Not only is action heard of here, but it is also heard of in the Veda; so he says: "having as its fruit the state of Indra and so forth. According to the rule, "One desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) should sacrifice with the *Vājapeya*" (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 18.1.1), self-sovereignty—that is, the state of Indra—is the fruit of that action. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), actions having heaven and other such things as their fruits, as well as prohibited acts such as the killing of a Brahmin which have hell as their fruit, are also heard of in scripture. That [action] is distinct.

"Separately," [means] "it produces birth"—this is the connection [of the words]. For it is impossible for actions with mutually contradictory results to produce a single birth simultaneously. Nor can it be maintained that even the destruction of the action [is possible], because one must necessarily accept that those [actions] persist in order to yield their results in another birth; thus, the doctrine of actions bearing fruit in this very life (*aihika-karmavāda*) is simply untenable. As it has been said: "If [the action] bears fruit..."
"Not all of that [karma] remains as a fixed, supreme experience at that very time" (Ślokavārttika, Citrākṣepaparihāra 26).
Now, by this much it has been stated that karma whose effects have already begun (*ārabdhakārya*) is simply not possible; who else says this? However—

By every human action, consisting of both dharma and adharma, which brings about its own fruit, it is the very *saṃskāra* of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) that is produced; for this is observed even in the case of human activity such as agriculture. That [action] is indeed initiated by that [activity], yet this *saṃskāra* depends upon its own maturation, depending on the exhaustion of the experience of the fruits of intense obstructive karma in certain cases.

Depending on the exhaustion of specific worldly enjoyments, whether accompanied by the assistance of opposing karmic fruits or acting alone, karma will at some time in a certain birth deliver its fruit to the person like a deposited treasure; thus, the diversity of the ripening of karma cannot be determined by those who are not omniscient. Therefore, because karma that yields fruit in another birth is possible, it is exactly as previously stated.
The state of being a Kevalin belongs only to those liberated according to the Sāṃkhya system. || 54 ||
[Objection: But surely even in your own scripture, the state of isolation (kaivalya) of the self is heard of; how so? He says:

"In the world [measured by] the size of a thumb, isolation may occur for the bound soul (paśu) through discernment (vijñāna), yoga, renunciation (saṃnyāsa), or from the exhaustion of karma through experience. (55)

In the world-sphere of *kalā*, which is the dwelling place designated as being the size of a thumb and so forth, [one attains liberation] either through discernment (*vijñāna*) regarding the distinction between *māyā* and the *puruṣa*, or through yoga consisting of the mastery of the mind aided by its limbs such as withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*),
or through renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) which has the fruit of the discernment of *māyā*, [and thus abandons] all action.

For one who has surrendered all actions to the Lord with the thought, "This is for the Lord," liberation (*kaivalya*)—which is caused by the complete cessation of the state of being an enjoyer—is possible precisely in that case through the exhaustion of all karma by means of the enjoyment of its fruits alone; it is not possible, however, according to what you have stated. || 55 ||
[The opponent objects: "But surely that very state of isolation (*kaivalya*) will be our liberation. To this he says:

"This Self has arisen for the sake of liberation; thus, the dissolution of the self is the fruit, because of the total exhaustion of the qualities of vision and action through their dissolution back into the material cause (*upādāna*). (56)
Even that which is desired as liberation—namely, absolute isolation (*kaivalya*)—is in fact the destruction of the self for you, because of the continued existence of impurity (*mala*).

On the contrary, like the state of non-existence (*akalāvasthā*), there is an absence of even limited knowledge and agency; for according to you, liberation is merely the dissolution of the unmanifest (*avyakta*) through the withdrawal of the *guṇas*, which results in the loss of the self.
Having thus refuted the Sāṃkhya position as well, he says to everyone in order to conclude:
"Those who claim that the flame is transferred are the greatest fools among the ignorant, for even their own selves are destroyed;
they are merely those who consider themselves wise among the knowers. (57)
All these proponents of doctrines, whose primary characteristic is delusion, must be avoided from afar by those seeking the highest good (*śreyas*).

For them, there is the notion that what is not the highest good—namely, the destruction of the self or something similar—is indeed the highest good for others; the meaning is that, according to them, liberation (*mokṣa*) is not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) at all. To illustrate this, as stated in the *Mataṅgapārameśvaravṛtti* (on Viṣamapada 5.60–61): "Of the knower and the object of knowledge... [and so forth].
"This [statement] was cited by us elsewhere" refers to what is stated in the *Śivayogasāra* (p.

33). It is recorded as being "stated in the *Mantravārttika-ṭīkā*" (p. 125, note 19, which should be consulted there). Or rather, because of the absence of cognition for all disputants, liberation would be equivalent to the destruction of the self, even if the state of being a knower were manifested.

"But in the other case... [Thus it is said]. Now, one might object: "For those who maintain the doctrine of transmigration (*saṃkrāntivādin*), there is no destruction of the self in liberation. To this he replies: "Those who consider themselves wise among knowers" refers to the *śikhā*, which is Power (*śakti*). Those proponents of transmigration are indeed unwise regarding liberation, because it has been stated that they are not liberated from this predicament: "For Śambhu alone knows and acts in all respects even therein" (verse 29). || 57 ||

If this is so, since all liberation treatises are sublated like the [claims of] a liberated person and because they contradict one another, what validity do they possess? To this he says "it is not so":
"The others are deficient regarding reality, because they do not speak of [the state] beyond passion."
Therefore, because they have transcended illusion, those who know [the truth] abide in their abodes.

For it is not the case that every means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must have all objects as its domain; rather, other means of valid cognition are indeed valid precisely because they reveal only a limited number of objects, just like perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the others. To the question, "How is it that these [scriptures] reveal only a limited number of objects? he says:

"Because there is no teaching beyond [the stage of] passion (*rāga*). This refers to the collection of principles (*tattva-jāta*) beginning with passion and ignorance (*avidyā*), along with the process (*prakriyā*) that follows them.

"Beyond that [level of *rāga*], consciousness [is characterized] by qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth. This word "beyond" (*ūrdhva*) has the same meaning as the word "above. Because they do not mention the entire collection of principles (*tattva*) beyond *rāga*, their vision is incomplete. To the question, "If this is so, what is attained through other scriptures? he says: "Because of the transcendence of *māyā* by that [means]. That which was not seen by them beyond *rāga*—by that [means, it is attained].

Below the principle of Māyā, those who know [the truth] and are liberated according to other philosophical systems (darśanāntara) are dissolved into the categories of principles, worlds, and aggregates. If it is asked, "Whose dissolution is into what?", this has been demonstrated in the presentation of the authority of the Āgamas. || 58 ||
In order to conclude his own section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*), he says:
"Thus, the fruits sung by the disputants have been stated briefly;
[this was done] so that students might not engage in the means for attaining those [fruits]. (51)
Thus ends the *Paramokṣanirāsakārikā* composed by the teacher Sadyojyotiḥśiva.

The fruits established by all disputants, which are characterized precisely as liberation, have been stated in brief. If it is asked for what purpose this was said, it is explained as follows: since people might engage in inferior fruits without having ascertained the scripture that establishes the means to the fruit, those seeking the highest good (*śreya*) should engage in this [scripture] alone by way of excluding what is not the yoga (*ayogavyavaccheda*). For from this, the supreme state of ultimate bliss (*niḥśreyasa*) is attained.

"It is accomplished. This [is stated] according to the view of the author of the *Gauravavṛtti*; for, by way of the sequence of initiation (*dīkṣākrama*), all the *kārikās* contained within the *Anyāgamamokṣadūṣaṇa* are not [included here] due to their profundity.
Since these [treatises] were indeed only partially fathomed by those of limited knowledge, Rāmakaṇṭha— the son of Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha— has clearly composed this *Viveka* (Commentary) upon them.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Paramokṣanirāsakārikā*, composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha.
